Iſa. 30.30, 31. and in the Roman hiſtorie, when Marcus Antonius the Philoſopher fought with the Quades, ([ilegible]) and by the praiers of the thundering legion (as they were afterwards called) of the Chriſtians rain was obtained to the refreſhing of the Roman armie, ingens grando compluraque fulmin[ilegible] in hoſtes ceciderunt: Itaque (Dio in vita M. Ant. Phil.) licebat videre in eodem loco aquam ignemque ſimul de coelo cadere, atque obcam cauſam, Romanos valere ac bibere. Quados exuri & penitùs interire. i. e. A huge hail and manie light-bolts fell upon the enemie: Fire and water fell at once from heaven, the Romans drank of the water and were relieved, the Quades were burn't by the fire, and periſhed.

entries.title: Exodus 9:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And break everie tree of the field! Here was ſtrages & clades horrenda, yet Pharaoh's heart is not broken, (Aug.) but remain's obdurate. Perdidiſtis fructum afflictionis, was an heavie charge. Ducklings ſtoop and dive at anie little ſtone thrown by a man at them; yet ſhrink not at the heavens great thunder.

entries.title: Exodus 9:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Onely in the land of Goſhen] See the note on chap. 8. ver. 23. Dio reports further of the fire forementioned, ver. 23. That that fire from heaven either fell not at all upon the Romans; or, if it did, it was preſently quenched: neither did the waters help the Quades, (Dio ubi ſuprà) but inflamed them as if it had been oil, ſo that they called for water to cool them, when the rain fell upon them; and wounded their own bodies to quench the fire with their blood.

entries.title: Exodus 9:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Lord is righteous] See the note on chap. 5. ver. 2.

entries.title: Exodus 9:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will let you go] But though hee ſpake thus fair, (Prov. 26.25.) believ him not: for there are ſeven abominations in his heart: No ſooner was Pharaoh off the rack, but hee bite's in his confeſſion, and retract's his promiſe.

entries.title: Exodus 9:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will ſpread abroad mine hands] viz In praier; holding up and out the palmes of the han[ilegible], as thoſe do that exſpect to receiv an almes, in a having manner: So did Solomon. 2 Chron. 6.13. See Pſalm. 143.6. Ezr. 9.9. [That the earth is the Lords] See the note on ver. 14.

entries.title: Exodus 9:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That yee will not yet fear] Howb[ilegible]it I will praie for you, and you ſhall feel the fruit of it. Thus God is good to the juſt and unjuſt. Matt. 5.

entries.title: Exodus 9:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But ſinned yet more] As iron is verie ſoft and malleable, while in the fire: but ſoon after return's to its former hardneſs. So here.

entries.title: Exodus 10:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: AS hee that bring's in a light, blinde's an Owl; or as hee that powr's on water kindle's the Lime whereupon it is powred: ſo the Lord by publiſhing his commands and by doing his miracles hardened the heart of Pharaoh; who, for his wilful rebellion was juſtly forſaken of God, and delivered up to his own heart, which is ſomwhat worſ them to bee delivered up to the divel.

entries.title: Exodus 10:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And that thou maieſt tell] The memorie of God's (magnalia) great works muſt bee tranſmitted to poſteritie: Ʋt nati natorum & qui naſcentur ab illis, that after-Ages may hear and fear this great God. See 1 Sam. 4. ver 8.

entries.title: Exodus 10:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How long wilt thou refuſe] God think's long of the time that men miſſpend and waſte in wicked courſes Jer. 4.14. and 13.27. It is a ſavorie ſaying of Bernard, Totum vitae meae tempus perdidi, quia perditè vixi: the time of my looſneſs I have utterly loſt.

entries.title: Exodus 10:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Elſ if thou refuſe] Men ſhould look up with David, and ſee the puniſhing Angel over their heads with a drawn ſword, and ſubmit. As if not Balaam's A[ilegible]s ſhal condemn them for their deſperate Lewdneſs: for hee fell down before the Angel. (Si qu[ilegible]ties peccent homiues, &c.) [I will bring the locuſts] God hath treaſuries of plagues for the obſtinate, neither c[ilegible]n hee bee (as the Poet feared of his Jupiter) poſſibly exhauſted.

entries.title: Exodus 10:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they ſhall cover] For they go forth by heaps. Pro. 30.27. and huge multiudes. Jud 6.5. [And ſhall eat everie tree] See Joel 1.7. Plin. lib. 11. cap. 29.

entries.title: Exodus 10:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And hee turned himſelf] No man may turn himſelf to go out of the great Turk's preſence, (Turk. Hiſt.) but muſt go backward till hee bee out of the room. Diſſention talling out between Queen Elizabeth and the Earl of Eſſex about a fit man for Government of Ireland, hee uncivilly turned his back, as it were in contempt with a ſcornful look: (Camden's Eliſ. fol. 494.) Shee, waxing impatient, gave him a cuff on the ear; bidding him com again when ſhee ſent for him, &c. But Moſes may not bee imagined to have ſo turned himſelf.

entries.title: Exodus 10:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Pharaob's ſervants ſaid unto him] They were convinced and mollified, though hee was not. Whom Hee will God hardeneth. Rom 9.18. [How long ſhall this man bee a ſnare unto us?] Hee was not the ſnare, but their own ſin. Pre. 29.6. Howbeit hee muſt bear the blame. As if ſom ſond people ſhould accuſe the Herald or the Trumpet as the cauſ of their war: oras if ſom ignorant peaſant, when hee ſee's his fowls bathing in his Pond, ſhould crie out of them as the cauſſes of foul weather.

entries.title: Exodus 10:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes and Aaron were brought, &c.] Somthing the tyrant would ſeem to yield to his Counſellors, and not to deal by them as the Perſian Monarchs, who were wont to adviſe with their Peers: but if anie of them delivered that which was contrarie to the King's minde, flagris caedebantur, (Keckerman.) they were whipped: which is a puniſhment alſo uſually inflicted at this daie by the great Turk, even upon the greateſt Baſſa's of the Court, (Tu[ilegible]k. Hiſt.) upon the leaſt diſpleaſure.

entries.title: Exodus 10:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For wee muſt hold a Feaſt] See the Note on Exodus 5. ver. 1.

entries.title: Exodus 10:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let the Lord bee ſo with you] In curſing them, hee unwittingly bleſſed them. Exod. 12.30, 31. and 13.21, 22. See Pſal. 109.28. Curſing men are Curſed men. But God's people fare the better for beeing curſed. Let them curſ but do thou bleſs, is not more a Praier then a Prophecie.

entries.title: Exodus 10:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Even all that the hail hath left] How eaſily can God ſtraiten, yea, ſtarv us all, if hee but ſend forth his forraging Armies. Joel 1.6.

entries.title: Exodus 10:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An Eaſt-winde] The proper and ordinarie office whereof is to purge the air.

entries.title: Exodus 10:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the locuſts went up] As a formidable armie: ſee a graphical deſcription of a like plague threatned. Joel 2.4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.

entries.title: Exodus 10:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I have ſinned againſt the Lord]. A fair confeſſion, but forced and extorted. Thus the toad, if beaten on the bellie, will vomit up his venom, and the malefactor on the rack will utter all. But as water heated, if taken off the ſire, (Ariſtot. Meteor. 1.12.) will ſoon return to its natural coldneſs, yea becom colder after heating then before; ſo hypocrites heats are not kindely from the Spirit, but violent from the outward fire of God's judgments: therefore when that is out, theſe are gone.

entries.title: Exodus 10:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Now therefore forgive] Moſes muſt forgive his ſin: God is not in all his thoughts. David crie's peccavi Pharnob perii: David, Againſt Thee, Thee onely have I ſinned: Pharaoh crie's to Moſes to pardon his ſin. Man may forgive the treſpaſs, but God onely the tranſgreſſion.

entries.title: Exodus 10:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And hee went out] The wiſdom from above is gencle, eaſie to bee intreated, readie to everie good work. The Divels are called Shegnirim, rough and rugged.

entries.title: Exodus 10:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A mightie ſtrong Weſt-winde] Rupertus call's the windes mundi ſcopas, the beeſoms wherewith God ſweep's his great houſ of this world: Like as his ſpiritual houſe (the hearts of his people) hee ſweep's off all foul luſts (thoſe helliſh locuſts) with that ruſhing mightie winde ſpoken of. Act. 2.2.

entries.title: Exodus 10:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But the Lord hardned] See the Note on ver. 1.

entries.title: Exodus 10:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Stretch out thy band] Here was no warning. See Exod. 8.16. as good, the more unexſpected, is the more welcom; ſo evil the more ſudden, the more terrible.

entries.title: Exodus 10:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They ſaw not one another] That they might know the worth of light, by the want of it. One being asked whither light was pleaſant? ([ilegible].) anſwered, That's a blinde man's queſtion. Little do wee prize this excellent creature.

entries.title: Exodus 10:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Called unto Moſes] viz. when the darkneſs was over: though ſom think that, even during the darkneſs, Pharaoh (ſuch was his madneſs) raged againſt God, and menaced Moſes.

entries.title: Exodus 10:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou muſt give us alſo ſacrifices] God gave Noah of everie clean beaſt ſeven (for ſacrifice likely) but of everie unclean two onely. Gen. 7.2.

entries.title: Exodus 10:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not an boof] God's Law muſt bee kept as the apple of our cie. Prov. 7.2. A diſpenſatorie conſcience is an evil conſcience. Repentance make's clean work: as the Flood drown'd all, even Noab's friends alſo.

entries.title: Exodus 10:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Get thee from mee] Evermore when God's meſſengers are abandoned, deſtruction is at next door by. I know that the Lord hath a purpoſe to deſtrole thee. See 2 Chron. 36.16.

entries.title: Exodus 10:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou haſt ſpoken well] q.d. When I ſee thee next, do thy pleaſure by mee. This was an act of faith in him, whereby hee feared not the wrath of the King. ([ilegible]) Heb. 11.27. So when Valens the Arrian Emperor threatned Baſil with bonds and baniſhment, Pueris illa terriculamenta proponat, ſaid hee, Let them threaten boies with thoſe fray-bugs. The Emperor may take away my life, but not my faith; my head, but not my crown.

entries.title: Exodus 11:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: WHo, after the hardneſs of his impenitent heart treaſured up to himſelf wrath. Rom. 2.5. God ſtrike's ſtill upon the thick boſſes of his b[ilegible]ckler. Job. 15.26. When men are no whit better by afflictions, and worſ with admonitions, God finde's it time to ſtrike home.

entries.title: Exodus 11:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Borrow of his neighbor] This was an extraordinarie command, and may not bee made a preſident but in the ſame caſe, and upon the ſame warrant. The Law-giver onely can diſpenſ with his own Law. Ordinarily it is the wicked that borroweth, and paieth not again. Pſal. 37.21.

entries.title: Exodus 11:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Was verie great in the Land of Egypt] Great hee was both in gift and autoritie; ſo that for his ſake the Iſraëlites might have what they would of the Egyptians: It was not here as once at Rome, Calamitas noſtra Magnus eſt: Sic Mimus olim de Pompeio, plaudente populo Romano tam eleganti ſoloeciſmo.

entries.title: Exodus 11:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes ſaid] ſ[ilegible]il. before hee went out of Pharaoh's preſence: for afterwards hee ſaw his face no more. chap. 10. ver. 29.

entries.title: Exodus 11:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That ſitteth upon his throne] As co-partner in the Kingdom. Our Henrie the ſecond crowned his eldeſt ſon Henrie, while hee was yet alive. But this young King, through diſcontent, fell into a fever, whereof hee died before his father; who caſt him away firſt by his indulgence, and after by his rigor, not ſuffering him to bee what himſelf had made him. [That it behinde the Mil] The hand-mil, which they drove before them. Judg. 16.21. Iſa. 47.2. Mat. 24.41.

entries.title: Exodus 11:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Agreat crie] Becauſ in everie houſ there ſhal bee a dead corpſ, and ſo a Conclamatum eſt. They had made Iſraël crie: and God uſually retaliate's ſpoil to ſpoil. Exek. 39.10. number to number. Iſa. 65.11, 12. choice to choice. Iſa. 66.3, 4. crie to crie. Jam. 5.1, 4. &c.

entries.title: Exodus 11:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall not a dog move his tongue] And yet how many dead dogs do now adaies bark and ſnarl at the Iſraël of God? (Canina ſacundia.) which, nevertheleſs, is not without God. 2 Sam. 16.9, 10. who will one daie make iniquitie to ſtop her mouth. Job 5.16. Why ſhould this dead dog curſ? ſaid Abiſhal.

entries.title: Exodus 11:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In a great anger] Heb. In heat of anger▪ wherewith in the cauſ of God hee was bleſſedly blown up. Meekneſs here had been but mopiſhneſs.

entries.title: Exodus 11:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That my wonders] See the note on Rom. 9.17.

entries.title: Exodus 11:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Did all theſe wonders] But all was worſ then ſpilt upon him: he was even ſet in ſin, and reſolved never to remove; God had a hand in it.

entries.title: Exodus 12:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: BEfore the ſlaughter of the firſt-born, yea before that plague was threatned. See Mr Torſhel his deſign for harmonizing the BIBLE.

entries.title: Exodus 12:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This moneth] Called Abib. Exod. 13.4. with us called March or April; when the daie lengthning, and the Sun aſſeending, each thing begin's to revive: To ſhew, ſaith one, that by the true paſſover Chriſt JESUS, not onely is our time and all other things ſanctified, but alſo that wee ſhould in recent remembrance of that benefit of our Redemption, all our daies and years bee thankful to our gracious Redeemer, and that by his death, true life and reviving unto mankinde. [It ſhall bee the firſt moneth] viz. in reſpect of ſacred, not civil affairs, as Junius here prooveth out of Joſephus. (Antiq. lib. 1. cap. 4.) The Jubi[ilegible]es began in September. Lev. 25.8. Exod. 23.16, 9, 10. The Creätion of the world began then, as ſom will have it: but Luther and others think it was in the Spring rather.

entries.title: Exodus 12:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In the tenth daie] The Paſchal-Lamb was taken up the tenth daie, but not ſacrificed till the fourteenth, that they might ſo kill the paſſover as firſt to ſanctiſie themſelvs and prepare their brethren. (Hoſpin. de crig. [ilegible]eſt. cap. 5.) 2 Chron. 35.6. For which cauſ alſo it was a received tradition among the the Jewes, that during thoſe four daies the Lamb was tied to their bed poſts.

entries.title: Exodus 12:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall make your count] ſeil. of Communicants; that the whole may bee eaten up, and everie one have enough. Spiritual bleſſings may bee divided in ſolidum, one may have as much as another, and all alike. The Gentiles alſo are called to fruition and feeding on the Lamb.

entries.title: Exodus 12:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Without blemiſh] Chriſt that immaculate Lamb of God was hereby typified. 1 Pet. 1.19. See the Note there. [From the ſheep, or from the goats] A lamb, to ſhew Chriſt's innocencie, meekneſs, patience, profitableneſs. Or a kid, to ſhew that hee was a ſinner: 1. By Imputation, for God made our ſins to meet upon him. Iſa. 53.6. 2. By Reputation, for hee made his grave with the wicked, ver. 9.

entries.title: Exodus 12:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋntil the fourteenth daie] See the note on ver. 3. [In the evening] Chriſt came in the evening of the world. Heb. 1.2. in the laſt hour. 1 Job. 5. when all laie buried in darkneſs; in the even-tide of our ſin and death.

entries.title: Exodus 12:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And ſtrike it on the two ſide-poſts] Not on the threſhold. Wee may not tread under foot the Son of God, or count the blood of the Covenant an unholy thing. Heb. 10.29. but get our hearts ſprinkled therewith by the hyſop-bunch of Faith from an evil conſcience, that wee may ſerv the living God. Heb. 9.14.

entries.title: Exodus 12:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In that night] By candle-light: ſo muſt wee feed upon Chriſt, lumine ſupernaturali: (Iſa. 53.) by his knowledg doth God's righteous ſervant juſtifie manie. [Roſt with fire] Not raw: wee may not groſly conceiv of Chriſt, nor raſhly receiv him. Not boiled, bur roſt: to ſhew that Chriſt was roſted in the fire of his father's wrath: & ſicut toſtis cibariis non adhibentur alia, ut in [ilegible]lixis fieri conſuevit: it à ſolum Chriſtum debemus apprehendere fide, (Alſted.) ſaith an Interpreter. [And unleavened bread] See the Note on 1. Cor. 5.7, 8. [And with bitter herbs] To teach, that looking upon Chriſt whom they have pierced men muſt bee in bitterneſs. Zach. 12.10. and feel what an evil and bitter thing ſin is. Jer. 2.19. beeing readie to ſuffer hardſhip with Chriſt, though hee ſhould feed us to the full with bitter herbs, and make us drunk with wormwood. Lam. 3.15.

entries.title: Exodus 12:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: His head with his legs] To let us ſee our need of whole Chriſt, and our moſt perfect comunion with Him.

entries.title: Exodus 12:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And yee ſhall let nothing of it remain] Wee may not preſume to ſin in hope of pardon. Chriſt will not ſtand us for a ſinning-ſtock.

entries.title: Exodus 12:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With your loins girt] As preſt and intent to the ſervice: ſo wee ſhould bee at all times, but eſpecially when to depart out of the F[ilegible]ypt of this life, and to take heaven by force. Then, if ever, wee ſhould hoc agere, gird up the loins of our minds, &c. 1 Pet. 1. [And yee ſh[ilegible]ll [ilegible]at it in haſt] As not doubting of deliverance, and waiting a call out of life. [It is the Lord's paſſover] A ſacramental expreſſion, like that of our Savior, This is my bodie. Mat. 26.26. ſee the Note there. The ſacraments of the old Teſtament were both ſaeraments and types: but thoſe of the New, are ſacraments onely.

entries.title: Exodus 12:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And will ſmite all the firſt-born] This croſſeth not that in Ezek. 18. The ſon ſhall not bear the iniquitie of his father: for God never puniſheth the innocent, becauſ all are guiltie before Him. Theſe Egyptians had ſlain Iſraël God's firſt-born. And it is the obſervation of Theodoret, that when God ſmote Pharaoh's firſt-born, hee drew blood of the arm for the cure of the head: which becauſ it mended not thereupon, came alſo to confuſion. [and upon all the Gods of Egypt] As hee did here upon the Popiſh Idols in the begining of the Reformation, by detecting their vanitie and laying their honor in the duſt.

entries.title: Exodus 12:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will paſs over you] Or, over-skip you. So hee dealeth oft by his, who ſhould therefore keep a paſſover for our ſafetie.

entries.title: Exodus 12:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By an Ordinance for ever] Till Chriſt our paſſover ſhould bee ſacrificed for us; and then the Chriſtian paſſover was to ſucced.

entries.title: Exodus 12:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yee ſhall put away leaven] All unſoundneſs in point of Faith, and inſinceritie in point of Practice. See the Note on 1 Cor. 5.7.

entries.title: Exodus 12:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An boli[ilegible] convocation] This ſame word (in the Hebrew) ſignifieth the holie Scriptures; (Nehem. 8 9.) to teach us, ſaith one, that the Scriptures ought to be read in the Congregation, and holie Aſſemblies.

entries.title: Exodus 12:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In this ſelf-ſame daie] Heb. In the bodie or ſtrength of this daie: ſo the mid-daie is called. Art thou delivered, helped? write up the time and place.

entries.title: Exodus 12:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋntil the ane and twentieth dai[ilegible]] As Auſtin ſaid of the feaſt of Pentecoſt, might theſe of the Paſſover, may wee of the Powder plot; Gaudet produci haec ſolemnitas. It were well i[ilegible] this holie-daie were a double-daie.

entries.title: Exodus 12:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: No leaven found] See the Note on ver. 15. [Shal bee cut off] For a ſmal fault, as it may ſeem to ſom: but the leſs the matter, the greater is the contempt in denying to do it. Keep therefore God's commandement as the ſight of thine eie. Look to thoſe minntula Legi[ilegible], that yee may live.

entries.title: Exodus 12:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yee ſhal eat nothing leavened] Watch carefully againſt corruption in life and doctrine: bee punctual in your preparation to, and participation of the Chriſtian paſſover.

entries.title: Exodus 12:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All the elders of Iſraël] The maſters of Families; who in this Familie-ſervice were to kill and eat, and ſet before the reſt of the houſhold, as prieſts at home; and to ſhew them the meaning of that myſterie.

entries.title: Exodus 12:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A bunch of hyſop] An herb of a purging propertie. See 1 Cor. 6.11. [The blood that is in the baſon] The remembrance of Chriſt's bloodie paſſion muſt bee kept freſh in our hearts. [Strike the lintel] Profeſs Chriſt crucified, (T[ilegible]m recent mil[ilegible]i nunc Chriſtus ac ſi hac borâ [ilegible] diſſ[ilegible]t ſanguinem. Luth.) honor him by a holie converſation, minde him in your out-goings and in comings [None of you ſhal go out] Bee not of thoſe that withdraw to perdition, but of them that believ to the ſalvation of the ſoul. Heb. 10.39. Mingle no more with the Egyptians.

entries.title: Exodus 12:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Will not ſuffer the deſtroier] Angels delight to bee executioners of God's judgments, and Saviors of his people.

entries.title: Exodus 12:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For ever] See the Note on ver. 15.

entries.title: Exodus 12:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yee ſhal keep this ſervice] yet with ſom variation of circumſtance.

entries.title: Exodus 12:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When your children] Children are to bee carefully catechiſed and informed. Eph. 6.4. See the note there. Luther ſcorned not to profeſs himſelf diſcipulum Catechiſmi, a Catechiſm Scholar.

entries.title: Exodus 12:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bowed the head] In token of ſubmiſſion to the command and thank fulneſs for ſuch a ſalvation.

entries.title: Exodus 12:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Went away and did &c.] They that will not timouſly obeie God's ſweet precepts, ſhal one daie have no other command to obeie but that bitter, Ite maledicti, Go yee curſed, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 12:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: From the firſt-born of Pharaoh] See ver. 12.

entries.title: Exodus 12:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For there was not an houſ] Neither is there an houſ amongſt us (hardly) where not one, but manie are dead in treſpaſſes and ſins. Our land even ſtink's again with ſuch, as Egypt did with the frogs.

entries.title: Exodus 12:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And bee called for Moſes] That is, hee ſent them to bee packing. See chap. 10.29.

entries.title: Exodus 12:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bleſs mee alſo] So Maximinus the Perſecutor beeing ſorely diſeaſed, ſent to beg the praiers of the Church. In their moneth you ſhal finde theſe wilde aſſes. Jer. 2.24.

entries.title: Exodus 12:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Wee bee all dead men] Quis autem vult mori? prorſus nemo. ([ilegible]. Ariſtot.) Everie thing make's much of life, from the higheſt Angel to the loweſt worm.

entries.title: Exodus 12:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they borrowed] For their uſe at that ſolemn feaſt they were to keep in the wilderneſs: (Pons aureus fugient[ilegible] hoſtiextr[ilegible]e[ilegible]du[ilegible].) The Egyptians denied them nothing; as willing to bee rid of them upon anie terms.

entries.title: Exodus 12:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Spoiled the Egyptians] See the note on chap. 8.2.

entries.title: Exodus 12:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: About 600000] So that promiſe to Abraham was fulfilled Gen. 15.14. and that to Jacob. Gen. 46.3.

entries.title: Exodus 12:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And a mixed multitude] Of ſtrangers, that took hold of the skirts of theſe Jews and ſaid, Wee will go with you. Zac[ilegible]. 8.23. but aferwards turned tippet. Num. 11.4. luſted greatly and greedily; and made Iſraël to ſin. Coals touched, will either burn or ſullie us.

entries.title: Exodus 12:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they baked unleavened cakes] A memorial of which ſweet mercie they kept on foot by that yearly feaſt of unleavened cakes. Deut. 16.3.

entries.title: Exodus 12:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Was four bundred and thirtie years] ſcil. from the time that Abrabam began to ſojourn in the Land of Canaan, and to paſs into Egypt. Gen. 12.10. See Gal. 3.17. with the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 12:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Even the ſelf-ſame daie] God (ſaith one) had wellnigh forfeited his bond; but e're the Sun went down hee paied the debt. His promiſes are good ſure-hold. At midnight the firſt-born were ſlain, becauſ then exactly the four hundred and thirtie years were exſpired.

entries.title: Exodus 12:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is That night] That, with an accent. God, expect's our returns ſhould bee anſwerable to our receipts. God's bleſſings are binders: and of all things hee can leaſt abide to bee forgotten.

entries.title: Exodus 12:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There ſhall no ſtranger, &c.] Strangers are excluded; to ſhew, that the faithful onely have fellowſhip with Chriſt; contra quam Lutherani ineptiunt, ſaith one.

entries.title: Exodus 12:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When thou hast circumeiſed him] And ſo admitted him into the fellowſhip of the faithful. A man muſt live before hee can bee nouriſhed, bred, before hee can bee fed.

entries.title: Exodus 12:45
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A forreigner] Unleſs a Proſelyte.

entries.title: Exodus 12:46
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In one bouſ] To teach them unitie; which indeed is not anie where found, but in the Church. Cam. 6.9. My Dove is but one, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 12:47
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall keep it] or periſh for their neglect. Aut faciendum aut patiendum: either men muſt do it, or die for it.

entries.title: Exodus 13:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: BY right of Redemption alſo. Hee that is ſaved is not his own, but his that ſaved him. Servati ſumus ut ſerviamus. Luk. 1.74.

entries.title: Exodus 13:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Remember] Heb. To remember indefinitely, q. d. Remember perpetually, and commemorate.

In the moneth Abib] The flowrie-moneth, as Macarius call's it. See the Note on chap. 12.2.

entries.title: Exodus 13:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Aland flowing with milk and honie] Where fulneſs may breed forget fulneſs ſaturitie, ſecuritie.

entries.title: Exodus 13:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Seven daies] Figuring our whole life.

entries.title: Exodus 13:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on chap. 12.19.20.

entries.title: Exodus 13:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And thou ſhalt ſhew] See the Note on chap. 12.26.

entries.title: Exodus 13:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And for a memorial] See the Note on Mat. 23.5.

entries.title: Exodus 13:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The males ſhall bee the Lords] This God did, that with the firſt-born ſon (commonly beſt beloved) hee might draw all the love to himſelf.

entries.title: Exodus 13:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And every firſtling of an Aſs] This God would not have paid him in kinde, eò quòd Aſinus tardum & pigrum animal, (Tuſc. Quaeſt. lib. quinto.) as Bellarmine give's the reaſon The zealous God hate's dulneſs. Tardis mentibus virtus non facilè committitur.

entries.title: Exodus 13:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That thou ſhalt ſaie unto him] Plantas tenellas frequentiùs adaquare proderit: (Primaſ. Greg. Mag.) young plants muſt bee often watered.

entries.title: Exodus 13:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That God led them not] Hee carefully choſe their waie out of Egypt; not the nearer, but the ſafer. Hee tempt's not above what wee are able: but ſo order's the matter, that evils are not readie for us. till wee for them.

entries.title: Exodus 13:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: God led the people about] Philo writeth that it was not much above three d[ilegible]ies iournie from Egypt to Canaan the next waie: Sed Dei volu tas eſt ſumma neceſſitas. (Tertul.)

entries.title: Exodus 13:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: From Su[ilegible]ot[ilegible]] their firſt Rendevouz chap. 12.37.

entries.title: Exodus 13:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the [ilegible]ord] See Pſal. 105.39. Iſa. 4.5, 6. God prot ct's, direct's and everie waie ſuit's the neceſſities of his people.

entries.title: Exodus 14:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: IT was of God then, (Neceſſe eſt adeſſe divinum ubi bumonum ceſſat auxilium. Philo Jud.) then that the people fell into ſuch ſtraits: that where humane help failed, divine might com in.

entries.title: Exodus 14:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That they turn] i.e. return. In paſſing the red Sea, the Iſraëlites made a ſemicircle. Confer Exod. 13.20. with Num. 33.6. God muſt bee followed, though hee lead us through a maze or Labyrinth.

entries.title: Exodus 14:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They are intangled] Perplexed, intricated, they know not what to do, or which waie to turn. Enemies watch opportunities, but oft miſs of their meaning.

entries.title: Exodus 14:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And I will bee honored] By ſubduing this ſturdie Rebel, and bringing his violent dealing upon his own pate. Pſal. 7.16. (1 King. 13.) When the Prophet cried to Jeroboam's altar, it clave preſently aſunder. (Jer. 23.29.) But the mightie hammer of God's word, with ten miracles, gave ten mightie ſtrokes at Pharaoh's heart, and yet could finde no entrance. God will therefore now take another courſ with him.

entries.title: Exodus 14:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That the people fled] i. e. Ran quite awaie, without anie reſolution ever to return. This troubled the tyrant: Crowns have their cares. Little David like's his hook the better ever ſince hee ſaw the Court.

entries.title: Exodus 14:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Made readie his charet] To meet his deſtruction.

entries.title: Exodus 14:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: (Veget. lib. 1. [ilegible]ap. 24.) 600 choſen charets] They fought of old out of charrets arm'd with ſithes and hooks; which at firſt were a terror, and after a ſcorn.

entries.title: Exodus 14:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With an high hand] Bravely, boldly, in battle-raie, (not as run-awaies) in all comly equipage.

entries.title: Exodus 14:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But the Egyptians purſued]. And God made fair waie before them, till they came into the red ſea.

entries.title: Exodus 14:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For they were ſore affraid] Becauſ ſorely diſtreſſed: they ſaw no waie to eſcape, unleſs they could have gone up to heaven: which becauſ they could not, heaven came down to them (though unworthie) that God might get him a name. Iſa. 63.12, 14. The Iſraëlites herein were far more happie then thoſe antient Britains, who beeing greatly diſtreſſed by their Northern Enemies in the time of Valentinian the third, implo [ilegible]ed the aid of Aetius the Roman Prefect of Gaul, uſing theſe words: To Aetius thrice conſul the ſigh's of the Britains: (Daniels Chronicle.) and after thus they complain. The barbarous enemie beat's us to the ſea; the ſea beats us back to the enemie: between theſe two kindes of deaths, wee are either murthered or drowned. But their implorations prevailed not: Neither found they anie other remedie then what the Prince of Orange ſhewed to his ſouldiers at the battle of Newport; (Hiſt. of Netherl.) when they had the ſea on one ſide, and the Spaniards on the other: If, ſaith Hee, you will live, you muſt either eat up theſe Spaniards, or drink up this Sea.

entries.title: Exodus 14:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Becauſ there were no graves] Thus they rebelled at the ſea, at the red-ſea, yet hee ſaved them for his names ſake. Pſal 106.7.8.

entries.title: Exodus 14:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is not this the word] Invalidum omne naturâ querulum. Weak ſpirits are ever quarrelling and contending. (Seneca.)

entries.title: Exodus 14:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Stand ſtill and ſee the ſalvation] Thus God heard their crie at the red-ſea] Neh. 9.9. Though it were not the crie of faith, but of fright and perturbation. So hee heard the voice of the lad. Gen. 21.17.

entries.title: Exodus 14:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Yee ſhall hold your peace] i. e. Yee ſhall neither ſaie, nor do.

entries.title: Exodus 14:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Wherefore crieſt thou unto mee?] ſc. with inward groanings, without anie audible voice Moſes egit vocis ſilentium, ut corde clamaret. And God was readier to anſwer, then hee to ask. [Speak unto the children of Iſraël] q. d. (Auguſt.) Ther's ſomthing more to bee don then to praie. Ora & labora. Wee muſt not onely crave God's help, but bee forward in the courſ, whereby to make waie for God's help. [That they gforward] Though upon a manifeſt danger. This is an act of ſtrong faith, pure obedience.

entries.title: Exodus 14:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But lift thou up thy rod] This rod God make's uſe of, for the greater manifeſtation of his own power, and the gracing of his ſervant Moſes.

entries.title: Exodus 14:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When I have gotten mee honor] Made mee a name as at this daie. Neh. 9.10. For this hee was famous in far countries. Jethro (the firſt proſelyte to the Jewiſh Church) was hereby converted, ſaie the Rabbines. (1 Sam. 4.8.) And the Philiſtimes crie Woe unto us, theſe are the Gods that ſmote the Egyptians with all the plagues in the Wilderneſs.

entries.title: Exodus 14:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the Angel of God] Chriſt the Angel of God's preſence. See chap. 13.21. and 23.22. [Went behinde them] So the glorie of the Lord was their rereward. Iſai. 58.8. Hee will bee to his both Van and Rere▪ Iſai. 52.12.

entries.title: Exodus 14:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A cloud and darkneſs to them] See the Note on Heb. 12.2.

entries.title: Exodus 14:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: (Func; Chron.) And Moſes ſtretched out his hand] Of that Pſeudo-Moſes that coze[ilegible]ed manie credulous Jews of Creet into the mid[ilegible]ſt of the ſea, Anno. 434. See Funccius at that year. [And the waters were divided] So was that torrent of fire (if Ariſtotle may bee beleived) that ran from Aetna, (De mundo. cap. 6.) conſuming the countrie, and yet parted it ſelf; making a kinde of a lane for thoſe that ventured to reſcue their aged parents.

entries.title: Exodus 14:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Were a wall unto them] Everie main affliction is our red-ſea (ſaith One) which, while it threat's to ſwallow, preſerv's us.

entries.title: Exodus 14:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In the morning watch] God watcheth upon the evil to bring it upon his enemies, then when hee may do them a greateſt miſcheif. Dan. 9.14. Hee picketh his times for vengeance Iſai. 33.10. [The Lord looked upon the hoſt] Hoe ſet his eies upon them (as Paul did upon Elymas the ſorcerer) with higheſt offence, and utmoſt indignation. After which lightening follow's that terrible thunderclap, wherewith hee troubled them and took off their wheeles. See Pſal. 77.18, 19. and 18.15.

entries.title: Exodus 14:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For the Lord fighteth for them] Our late great ſucceſſes have extorted the like acknowledgments from ſom of Satan's ſworn ſwordmen: as at the diſſolution of the ſeige at Plimmouth.

entries.title: Exodus 14:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That the waters may com again.] By winde that God ſent. Exod. 15.10, The windes blow, the waters flow. Pſal. 147.18.

entries.title: Exodus 14:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Returned to his ſtrength] For by beeing divided, it had been weakened. ſi collidimur, frangimur. The daughter of diſſenſion is diſſolution.

entries.title: Exodus 14:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There remained not one of them] No more doth there of our ſubdued iniquities. Mic. 7.19. Peccata non redeunt. Wee ſhall ſee them no more, anie otherwiſe then theſe Iſraëlites did their enemies, dead upon the ſhore.

entries.title: Exodus 15:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: PReſently upon the deliverance, whiles their hearts were hot, and the mercie freſh. No part of the thank-offering might bee kept unſpent till the third day. Beneſits ſoon grow ſtale, and putreſie, as fiſh.

entries.title: Exodus 15:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will prepare him an habitation] Or I will adorn him, I will give him ornaments and trimmings. Such God account's our poor praiſes.

entries.title: Exodus 15:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Lord is a man of war] Yea hee alone is a whole Armie of men, Van and Rere both. Iſai. 52.12. Hee ſend's the ſword. Ezek. 14.17. Muſter's the men. Iſai. 13.4. Order's the ammunition▪ Jer. 50.25. Give's the victorie; Whence hee is here ſtyled by the Chaldee. The Lord and Victor of wars.

entries.title: Exodus 15:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In the red ſea] So called haply from that red man Eſau or Edom, who uſurped the dominion of that ſea, now called Sinus Arabicus.

entries.title: Exodus 15:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As a ſtone] So ſhall Rome. Rev. 15.5.

entries.title: Exodus 15:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hath daſhed in pieces] It is a fearful thing to fall into the puniſhing hands of the living God. Heb. 10.31. For who knoweth the power of his anger? Pſal. 90.11.

entries.title: Exodus 15:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That roſe up againſt thee] Becauſ againſt thine. There is a league offenſive, and defenſive, betwixt God and his people.

entries.title: Exodus 15:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And with the blaſt] In celebrating God's favors, wee muſt bee punctual and particular.

entries.title: Exodus 15:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The enemie ſaid I will] They made account all was their own, but were ſoon confuted, as were likewiſe Siſera, and Sennacherib. Where the begining of a buſineſs is con[ilegible]idence, the end is conſuſion.

entries.title: Exodus 15:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou did'ſt blow, &c.] Here it was that the Arm of the Lord put on ſtrength to cut Rahab, and wound the dragon. Iſai. 51.9.

entries.title: Exodus 15:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Who is like thee] One of the moſt ſtately deſcriptions of God that is found in holy-writ. God is to bee magnified: Wee muſt make room for him.

entries.title: Exodus 15:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The earth ſwallowed them] That is the ſea, which compaſſeth the earth about as a girdle: God having ſet the ſolid earth upon the liquid waters. See Jon. 2.6. Pſal. 24.2.

entries.title: Exodus 15:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋnto thy holie habitation] Canaan where God choſe to dwell. This Hee is ſaid alreadie to have don, becauſ hee would certainly do it. God's promiſes are his performances, and everie former mercie a pledg of a future.

entries.title: Exodus 15:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sorrow ſhall take hold] So it did. 1 Sam. 4.8. [Then the Dukes of Edom] See Deut. 2.4.

entries.title: Exodus 15:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The mightie men] See it fulfilled. Num. 22.3. [ſhall melt] So they did. Ioſh. 2.9, 10, 11.

entries.title: Exodus 15:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Till thy people paſs over] Over Jordan (as now they have don over the red ſea,) into Canaan.

entries.title: Exodus 15:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of thine inheritance] provided and purchaſed by thee for thy firſt-born, Iſraël.

entries.title: Exodus 15:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Lord ſhall reign] Gaudeo quòd Christus Dominus eſt: alioqui totus deſperâſſem, write's Miconius to Calvin, upon the view of the Churches enemies. The Lord Chriſt reigneth. Or elſ I had been out of all hope of better.

entries.title: Exodus 15:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For the horſ of Pharaob] A good ſoul is altogether unſatisfiable in ſanctifying God's name, and ſetting forth his goodneſs. Should I do nothing elſ all the daies of my life (ſaid that Martyr) yea as long as the daies of heaven ſhall laſt, (Act. & Mon.) but kneel on my knees and repete David's Pſalms, yet ſhould I fall infinitely ſhort of what I ow to God.

entries.title: Exodus 15:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Miriam] Souls have no ſexes: And if ſouls follow the temperament of their bodies (as Philoſophie ſaith they do) womens bodies conſiſt of rater roomes, of a more exact compoſition then mens do.

entries.title: Exodus 15:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sing yee to the Lord] This ſeem's to have been the burden of the ſong: as Pſal. 136.1.

entries.title: Exodus 15:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And found no water] Thirſt and bitterneſs was their firſt handſel in their voiage.

entries.title: Exodus 15:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They could not drink] Water they now had, but what the better? God can give us bleſſings, but with ſuch a tang, that wee ſhall have no great joie of them.

entries.title: Exodus 15:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: (Seneca.) Murmured againſt Moſes] Hee muſt bear the blame of all. Publick perſons are ſure to have an ill life of it. Qui vitaverit culpam, non effugit infamiam.

entries.title: Exodus 15:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shewed him a tree] A type of Chriſts ſweet croſs, and eaſie yoke, that ſweetneth and facilitateth all our light afflictions.

entries.title: Exodus 15:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And ſaid if thou, &c.] This God premiſeth as a preface to the law, to bee ſhortly after given in Sinai. [I am the Lord that healeth thee] Both on the inſide, by forgiving all thine iniquities, and on the outſide, by healing all thy diſeaſes. Pſal. 103. I am Jehovah the Phyſician. And omnipotenti medico nullus inſanabilis occurrit morbus. (Iſidor.) To an Almightie Phyſician no diſeaſ is uncurable.

entries.title: Exodus 15:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they came to Elim] The Heathens ſlandered the Jews, (Corn. Tacit. Annal. l. 12.) that they found theſe fountains by the means of certain aſſes that guided them: Whence they are called Aſinarij by Molon and Appion of Alexandria; who affirmed that for this cauſ the Jews worſhipped the golden head of an aſs, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 16:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SO called becauſ it bordered upon the citie of Sin, whereof ſee Ezek. 30.15.16. With Ezek. 20.35, 36. Or of the manie brambles that grew therein.

entries.title: Exodus 16:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the whole Congregation] The moſt part of the people. Diaconos paucitas honorabiles fecit, ſaith Hierom: ſic & veros Iſraëlitas.

entries.title: Exodus 16:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To kill this whole Aſſemblie] Thus diſcontent will ſaie anie thing: neither careth it how true the charge bee, but how ſtinging and ſtabbing.

entries.title: Exodus 16:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will rain bread from heaven] Not hell from heaven, as once hee did upon Sodom. If thine enemie hunger, feed him, as God here doth.

entries.title: Exodus 16:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: On the ſixth daie they ſhall prepare] The Jews preparation to the Sabboth began at three a clock in the afternoon. (Buxtorf. Synagog.) The beſt and wealthieſt of them, even thoſe that had manie ſervants, did with their own hands further the preparation: So that ſomtimes the maſters themſelvs would chop hearbs, ſweep the houſ, cleav wood, kindle the fire, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 16:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That the Lord] And not wee without his autoritie: ſo that in murmuring againſt us, yee have ſet your mouthes againſt heaven. Caveant [ilegible] Grudg not, behold the Judg ſtandeth before the doore.

entries.title: Exodus 16:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: (Jam 5.9.) Yee ſhall ſee the glorie of the Lord] Shining in that wonderful work of his, the bread from heaven. Confer Num. [ilegible]4.21. I[ilegible]b. 11.40.

entries.title: Exodus 16:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In the evening fleſh to eat &c] Never was Prince ſo ſerved in his greateſt pomp, as theſe rebellious Iſraëlites. How good ſhall wee finde him then to thoſe that pleat him?

entries.title: Exodus 16:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For hee hath heard your murmurings] Now then what will you do, ſith God riſeth up. And ſith hee vi[ilegible]teth, what will yee anſwer? I[ilegible]b. 31.14.

entries.title: Exodus 16:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Toward the wilderneſs] Where the cloud was in the forefront of their armies.

entries.title: Exodus 16:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the Lord ſpake] i. e. Hee [ilegible]ad before ſpoken.

entries.title: Exodus 16:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And in the morning] They have their fleſh at Even, and bread in th[ilegible] morning. God will bee waited on, and give the conſummation of his bleſſings at his leiſure. The cloud emptie's not it ſelf at a ſuddain burſt, but diſſolve's upon the earth, drop after drop.

entries.title: Exodus 16:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The dew laie round] i. e. The Manna that came down in the dew, as Chriſt the bread of life doth in the Miniſterie of the word. See Deut. 32.2.

entries.title: Exodus 16:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The dew that laie] And covered the Manna: whence that promi[ilegible]e of hidden Manna. Revel. 2.17.

entries.title: Exodus 16:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: (Lib: 26. cap. 14.) It is Manna] i. e. What ſhall I call? Herba Anonymus non inveniendo[ilegible]nomen, invenit, ſaith Plinie: ſo Manna. Others interpret Manna, a portion, an admirable gift, or meat prepared.

entries.title: Exodus 16:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Everie man according to his eating] Thus they were inured in diem vivere, as Quintilian ſaith the birds do, to de▪ pend upon God for their daily bread.

entries.title: Exodus 16:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Som more, ſom leſs] ecundùm proportionem arithmeticam, ſed non ſecundum proportionem ceome[ilegible]icam. as a man had more or leſs mouthes in his familie to [ilegible]eed.

entries.title: Exodus 16:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee that gathered much] See the Note on 2 Cor. 8.15.

entries.title: Exodus 16:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let no man leav of it, &c.] It was to bee gathered in the morning, and not kept till the morrow. I made baſte and delaied not, ſaith David. Pſal. 119 60.

entries.title: Exodus 16:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Left of it untill, &c.] Eit[ilegible]er through diſtru[ilegible], or curioſitie.

entries.title: Exodus 16:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It melted] Or putrefied, faded, diſolved. Som Papiſts derive their Maſs from this root: and well it may bee; nam per eam omnis pietas liquefacta eſt & diſſoluta, ſaith Rivet: for it is the utter bane of all good, as beeing a maſs or heap of abhominations.

entries.title: Exodus 16:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And told Moſes] As fearing that the people had not don ſo well, as indeed they did: or as deſirous of further direction.

entries.title: Exodus 16:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Laie up for you &c.] This is no plea for the Popiſh keeping of their breaden God in a pyx, for here was a command ſo to do, leſt the Sabbath ſhould bee profaned: but for the other, there is none.

entries.title: Exodus 16:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Till the morning] The Sabbath-morning wherein it putrified not, but continued ſound and ſavorie by the ſpecial hand of God; that they might keep the Sabbath; as it appear's here they did, before the Law given at Sinai. Papiſts preſs the ſanctification of the Sabbath as a meer humane inſtitution in religious worſhip. Our Anti-ſabbatarian Prelates took this text for an Anticipation onely, and made little account of the fourth commandment, which Spalato had taught them was don awaie, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 16:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Eat that to daie] So ſhall thoſe that labor in the Lord reſt, and feaſt in heaven. Thus the Rabbines moralize it.

entries.title: Exodus 16:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And it came to paſs] See the Note on ver. 20. Som unrulie beaſts (maſterleſs monſters) will bee breaking over the hedg: but the Law will hamper them.

entries.title: Exodus 16:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How long refuſe yee] The rulers are ſhent for the peoples unrulineſs. [To keep my commandments] For in breaking that one of the Sabbath, they had broken all: the whole Law is but one copulative. See Jam. 2.10.

entries.title: Exodus 16:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hath given you the Sabbath] And a great gift it was. Nehe. 9.14. Were it not for the weekly ſabbath wee ſhould all run wilde. [Abide yee everie man in his place] Sabbath coming from Shabath to ceaſ or reſt, hath ſom affinitie with Jaſhabh to ſit ſtill, and with Shabath to worſhip and give praiſ, to ſhew, that this reſt muſt be ſanctified: for elſ it is but Aſinorum ſabbatum, as One ſaith, the Sabbath of the Ox and Aſs. for theſe alſo muſt reſt.

entries.title: Exodus 16:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So the people reſted] According to their cuſtom, though probably intermitted for a ſeaſon in Egypt, dureing their hard ſervitude. (D. prideaux.) Sed rationem reddat qui poteſt (ſaith a learned Doctor) quare, ante legem promulgatam, in die ſeptimo ceſſavit Manna, niſi quia, ad exemplum Domini, ab ipſius mundi primordio invaluiſſet ſabbati obſervatio. This ceaſing of Manna on the ſeventh day ſhew's that the Sabbath was kept from the begining.

entries.title: Exodus 16:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the taſte of it] It had not all manner of good taſtes, according to everie man's appetite; as Wiſd. 16.20, 21. It is ſaid, but as Num. 11.8. Elſ why ſhould the people luſt and murmur, as there they did. ver. 4, 5.

entries.title: Exodus 16:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Fill an omer] Monuments and memorials of God's great mercies are to bee ſet up, leſt (as it fare's with children) Eaten bread bee ſoon forgotten. (Strabo Geog.)

entries.title: Exodus 16:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Take a pot] A golden pot. Heb. 9.4. Strabo writeth, that the Metapontini (after a plentiful harveſt which had much enriched them) dedicated to Apollo at Delphos [ilegible] an harvest of gold.

entries.title: Exodus 16:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To bee kept] For the uſe of ſucceeding ages, in the moſt holie places: ſo Chriſt, glorified in his humanitie, abide's for ever. Heb 7.

entries.title: Exodus 16:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋntill they came] So till wee com to heaven, ſhall wee have need of Ordinances.

entries.title: Exodus 16:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of an Ephah] Or of a buſhel: a plentiful allowance: ſee the Note on Ioh. 2.7.

entries.title: Exodus 17:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: AFter they had firs;t been at Dophcah, and at Aluſh. Num. 33.12, 13, 14. [There was no water] Bread they had from heaven, but wanted water. Our condition here is a condition of ſingular indigencie: wee are ever wanting ſomwhat, or other.

entries.title: Exodus 17:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The people did chide with Moſes] As they did before for bread. And as thirſt is the more eager appetite, ſo they are more eager and earneſt for water, then they were for bread, [Wherefore do yee tempt the Lord] viz Whether hee bee amongſt you, and bee able by miracle to reliev you.

entries.title: Exodus 17:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Murmured againſt Moſes] Magiſtrates have manie times a wearie life, with the mutinous multitude. Seneca obſerveth of Egypt (it proved true of this people newly com out of Egypt) that it was loquax & ingenioſa in contumeliam proefectorum provincia: in qua, qui vitaverit culpam, non effugit infamiam. That it was [ilegible] province apt to prate againſt their Governors, and to caſt a ſlur upon them, though never ſo well deſerving.

entries.title: Exodus 17:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Readie to ſtone mee] Well might hee ask with our Saviour, For which of my good works do yee ſtone mee? (John 10.32.) But the bellie hath no cars.

entries.title: Exodus 17:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Take with thee of the Elders] As witneſſes of this great work of God; which the people for their unbelief might not behold. God put's up their rebellion, and ſat is[ilegible]e's their thirſt: but yet intimates his juſt diſpleaſure, by denying them this privilege of ſeeing the rock ſmitten.

entries.title: Exodus 17:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋpon the rock] If God had not ſtood upon the rock, in vain had Moſes ſtruck it. Means muſt bee uſed, but God onely depended upon for ſucceſs. It is hee alone that ſet's the rock abroach. [Thou ſhalt ſmite the rock] Here in a type of Chriſt, ſtricken, ſmitten of God and afflicted. Iſa. 53.4. 1 Cor. 10.4. [And there ſhall com water out of it] Not ſire, (that had not been ſo miraculous,) but water. This cleaving the hard rock. Pſalm 78.15. This turning of the ſlint into a fountain. Pſalm 114.8. was a work of Omnipotencie, and is therefore much celebrated. Deut. 8.15. Pſalm 105.41 Nehem. 9 15. Dioſcorides tell's us of the ſtone Galactites, quèd ſuceum emittat lacieum, that it yield's a kinde of moiſture like milk which, if it bee true, is verie ſtrange. [That the peo[ilegible]le may d[ilegible]ink] And ſo bee cooled and comforted in their wearineſs and wandrings. Ho, everie one that thirſteth, &c. Iſa 55.1.

entries.title: Exodus 17:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is the Lord amongſt us?] As if that could not bee, and they athirſt? But hee is moſt preſent, when hee afflict's: Hee know's our ſouls in adverſitie.

entries.title: Exodus 17:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Then came Amalek] Not having the fear of God before his eles. Deut. 25.18. but carried on by the antient enmitie: for Amalek was Eſau's grandchilde.

entries.title: Exodus 17:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will ſtand on the top] Where the people might ſee him with that Enſign in his hand, and bee incouraged, Xerxes uſed to pitch his tent on high, and ſtand looking on his armie, when in fight, for their incouragement.

entries.title: Exodus 17:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Aaron and Hur] This Hur, ſaith Joſephus, was huſband to Miriäm, and Moſes his Deputie. Exod. 24.14. [Went up to the top of a hill] To praie together. Pſalm 76.2.3. In the Congregation where the Saints are praying, there the arrow, ſhield, and ſpear are broken. 2 Sam. 18.3. From thence ſhalt thou help us; (ſaid the people to David) that is, thy praiers ſhall prevail with God for our aſſiſtance. Non tam praeliando quàm precando. The King of Sweden aſſoon as hee ſet foot in Germanie fell down to praier, and hee proved verie victorious.

entries.title: Exodus 17:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When Moſes held up his hands] The puſh of Moſes's praiers did more then the pikes of all Iſraël beſides. Moſes orat & vincit, (Bucholcer. Chronol.) ceſſat & vincitur, ſaith one. Great is the power of praiers. Henricus Anceps, the Emperor of Germanie, ſlew and put to flight a huge armie of the Hungarians, his ſouldiers all crying out with a loud voice, (Idem ibid.) Kyrie eleiſon, Kyrie eleiſon, i, e. Lord have mercie upon us, Lord have mercie upon us. This was don before the citie of Mersburg.

entries.title: Exodus 17:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But Moſes's hands were heavie] It is a praiſ proper to God, that his hand is ſtretched out still: As for men, even the beſt, though the ſpirit in them bee willing, yet the fleſh is weak, and will not ſuffer anie long intention. [And Aaron and Hur ſtaid up his hands] Neither did they onely raiſ up their hands, but their mindes with his. There are that here obſerv, that upon the fourtieth daie after their coming out of Egypt, Moſes, Aaron, and Hur went up into the Mount, where Moſes's hands are thus ſupported, while Amalek is diſcomfited; and that Moſes the Prophet, Hur the Prince, and Aaron the Prieſt, all put together, were a type of Chriſt; who on the fourtieth daie after his Reſurrection aſſcended into the Mount of Heaven; where, as our Prophet, Prieſt, and Prince, hee hold's up the hands of his Interceſſion for his Church Militant, whiles ſhee fight's with ſpiritual Amalek, Sin, Satan, Antichriſt, World, Fleſh, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 17:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Joſhua diſcomfited] How ſhould hee do otherwiſe, when hee fought with ſuch weapons? Praiers are the bombardae, & inſtrumenta bellica Chriſtianorum, ſaith Luther: The great guns, and warlike weapons of the Saints. The Romans in a great diſtreſs were driven to take the weapons out of the Temples of their gods, and overcame. The Parliament ſouldiers at Edg-hill-battle falling on with courage, and crying out, Now for the fruit of praier, Now for the fruit of praier; prevailed mightily, ſlaying near ten to one, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 17:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In a book] Or, in the book that thou art now in writing: viz. the Pentateuch, the moſt antient book that is extant. [I will utterly put out &c.] The portion of wicked men is to bee forgotten in the citie where they had ſo don, Eccleſ. 8.10. their memorie die's with them: or, if it bee preſerved, it ſtink's in keeping, and remain's as a curſ and perpetual diſgrace.

entries.title: Exodus 17:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes built an Altar] As a laſting monument of God's great Mercie in that firſt victorie. The Romans had a cuſtom, that the Conqueror in his triumphant chariot rode to the Capitol, and offered a white ox to Jupiter. (Liv lib 6. Decad 3.)

entries.title: Exodus 17:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Becauſ the Lord, &c.] Heb. The hand upon the throne of the Lord. God's hand is laid upon his own throne, as ſwearing to root out Amalek. Or Amalek's hand is lifted up againſt God's throne, that is the Church (called God's throne of glorie. Jer. 4.21. and crown of glorie. Iſa. 62.3.) therefore hee will have perpetual war with him. Tua cauſſa erit mea cauſſa, ſaid the Emperor Charls the Fifth to Julius Pflugius, who, beeing his Agent, had received wrong by the Duke of Saxonie; ſo ſaith God to all that belong to him.

entries.title: Exodus 18:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ANd thereby was converted, (ſaie the Rabbins) beeing the firſt Proſelyte to the Jewiſh Church that wee read of in in Scripture.

entries.title: Exodus 18:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: After hee had ſent her back] Becauſ ſhee was troubleſom with her peeviſhneſs, and a hinderance to the good work in hand. Chap. 4.25, 26. Sylla felix fuiſſet ni uxorem duxiſſet; Adrianus ni imperitâſſet. Moſes, both.

entries.title: Exodus 18:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In a ſtrange land] See the Note on Chap. 2.22.

entries.title: Exodus 18:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Eliezer] Or Lazarus. Wee ſhould write God's mercies upon the names of our children, or ſom other waies perpetuate the memorie of them.

entries.title: Exodus 18:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: At the Mount of God] Horeb, whither they were removed from Rephidim, though the remove bee not mentioned.

entries.title: Exodus 18:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And hee ſaid] That is, ſent him word: ſo God's meſſages to us are to bee received as his own immediate words. Hee that heareth you, heareth mee.

entries.title: Exodus 18:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And did obeiſance] Sr. Thomas More Lord Chancellor, would in Weſtminſter-hall beg his Father's bleſſing on his knees.

entries.title: Exodus 18:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All that the Lord bath don] It is not enough to relate God's mercies to us in the lump, and by whole ſale; but wee muſt inſtance the particulars both to God and men. [That had com upon them] Heb. Had found them; yet not without a providence. Job 5.6. God cut's us out our ſeveral conditions: it is his hand that finde's us when wee ſuffer ought.

entries.title: Exodus 18:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Jethro rejoiced] So muſt all Sion's ſons, Iſa. 66.10.

entries.title: Exodus 18:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Jethro ſaid &c.] Cheerfulneſs make's thankfulneſs. Luke 1.46. Jam. 5.13.

entries.title: Exodus 18:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Now I know] See the Note on Ver. 1. So the people knew that Jehovah was God. 1 King. 18.37. See 2 Cro. 33.13. [Hee was above them] God ſit's in the heavens. Pſal. 2.4. where hee ſee's that their daie is coming. Pſal 37.16. and mean while ſcorneth theſe ſcorners. Prov. 3. Fright's them, as hee did thoſe Syrians. 2 King. 7.6. Over-aw's them, as hee did Laban. Divert's them, as hee did Saul, Senacherib, &c. or otherwiſe defeat's them, as hee did Benhadad, diſcloſing their counſels, blaſting their deſigns, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 18:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Before God] i.e. as in his preſence, with reverence and godlie fear. To feed without fear is a foul fault. Jude 12. See my Common-place of Abſtinence.

entries.title: Exodus 18:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the people ſtood by Moſes] Beeing haply (as the French are ſaid to bee) verie litigious, and thereunto abuting Moſes's lenitie: whereas had they been ſoundly whipped (as among Mahumetans they are, that go to law for light [ilegible]att[ilegible]rs) there would have been but few and ſhort ſuits amongſt them. Sure it is, that if men's hearts were not bigger then their ſuits, there would not bee half ſo manie.

entries.title: Exodus 18:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What is this thing] A man by good counſel may becom an Angel; nay, a God to another. Alexander beeing requeſted by ſom Embaſſadors to ſhew them his treaſures, ſhewed them his faithful Counſellors.

entries.title: Exodus 18:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To enquire of God] For a divine ſentence is in the mouth of the Judg: therefore alſo the place of Judicature is called the holie place. Eccleſ. 8.10. Let thoſe that go to law inquire of God, and reſt in his will.

entries.title: Exodus 18:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When they have a matter] In our ordinarie ſuits there is, for the moſt part more malice then matter. The late Judg Dier, if there came anie ſuch trilling controverſies to bee tried before him, would uſually ſaie, That either the parties are wilful, or their neighbors without charitie, becauſ their ſuits were not quietly compromiſed.

entries.title: Exodus 18:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Is not good] Wee commonly ſaie, Hee that receiv's a curteſie, ſell's his libertie. But ſo did not Jethro.

entries.title: Exodus 18:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou wilt ſurely wear away] Heb. Fading, thou wilt fade, as a leaf that wanteth moiſture. Melanchthon was wont to ſaie, that none labored ſo hard as Travelling women, Magiſtrates, and Miniſters. Politici & Eccleſiaſtici labores maximi ſunt, ſaith Luther. Atterunt enim corpus, & tanquam ex imis medullis exhauriunt ſuccum.

entries.title: Exodus 18:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will give thee counſel] A Midianite counſel's Moſes: God hereby teacheth him humilitie.

entries.title: Exodus 18:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Out of all the people] Magiſtrates muſt bee drained from the dregs, ſifted from the bran of the ordinarie ſort of people. [Able men] Able and active, ſtrong and ſtouthearted, wealthie alſo, and well underlaied. See Jethro's Juſtice of Peace in a Sermon by Mr. Sam. Ward.

entries.title: Exodus 18:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So ſhall it bee eaſier, &c.] How thankleſs is their labor that do wilfully over-ſpend themſelvs in their ordinarie vocations?

entries.title: Exodus 18:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To their place] To the promiſed land, Or to their own homes, well apaid, and with good content.

entries.title: Exodus 18:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So Moſes hearkned] Of a meek man it is ſaid that a childe ſhall lead him Iſa 11.6. how much more ſo grave a counſellor as Jethro? (Dio. in Auguſto.) Auguſtus [ilegible] was over-joyed with the plain dealings of his friends and counſellors: as of Mecoenas.

entries.title: Exodus 18:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes choſe] Not without the peoples conſent. Deut. 1.13, 14.

entries.title: Exodus 18:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Into his own land] An honeſt man's heart is where his calling is: ſuch a one when hee is abroad is like a fiſh in the air; whereinto if it leap for recreation or neceſſitie, yet it ſoon return's to his own element.

entries.title: Exodus 19:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Place where were manie buſhes and briars. Here they received [ilegible]he Law, which like briars and brambles pricketh and pierceth the conſciences of evil livers. And this ſell out 430. years after the Promiſe made to Abraham; not to diſanul the Promiſe. Gal. 3.17. but to advance it: and, that guilt beeing diſcovered, and everie mouth ſtopped. Rom. 3.19. wee might acknowledg the riches of free Grace and Mercie.

entries.title: Exodus 19:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For they were departed] See the Note on Chap. 18.5.

entries.title: Exodus 19:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes went up] See the note on Chap. 3.6.

entries.title: Exodus 19:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: On Eagles wings] The Eagle beat's her young ones out of their ſluggiſh neſt, that they may learn to flie: there was ſomwhat to do to bring Iſraël out of Egypt. (Munſter. in Schol. in Deut. 32.11. ex R. Solomon.) The Eagle carrie's her young upon her wings (and not between her talons as other birds do) openly, ſafely, ſpeedily: So did God his Iſraël, beeing choice and charie of them all the waie; ſecuring them alſo from their enemies, who could do them as little hurt, as anie can do the Eagle's young, which cannot bee ſhot but through the bodie of the old one. Som by Eagles here underſtand Moſes and Aaron, who are ſo called (ſaie they) propter acumen intelligentiae & altitudinem vitae, for the ſharpneſs of their underſtanding, and the loftineſs of their lives. See the Note on Deut. 32.11.

entries.title: Exodus 19:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: If yee will obeie my voice indeed] As I am good to you indeed, and not in pretenſ or profeſſion onely. Nathanaël was an Iſraëlite indeed. John 1.47. And Caleb fulfilled after God (or fully followed him) ſo did not Solomon. 1 King. 11.6.

entries.title: Exodus 19:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A kingdom of Prieſts] A holie ſtate, ſuch as ſhall bee all ſatiated with fatneſs. Jer 31.14. See the Notes on 1 Pet. 2.9. & Rev. 1.6.

entries.title: Exodus 19:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Laid before their faces] Or plainly propoſed the minde of God: ([ilegible].) ſo did Paul. Acts 17.3. So muſt Miniſters.

entries.title: Exodus 19:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All that the Lord hath ſpoken] Sed, quid dignum tanto feret hic promiſſor bia[ilegible]u? How eaſily over-ween wee our own abilities? Pollicitis dives quilibet eſſe poteſt. Words are good cheap.

entries.title: Exodus 19:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And believ thee] Without ſuſpicion of an impoſture; ſuch as was that of Mahomet.

entries.title: Exodus 19:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sanctifie them to daie, and to morrow] Men muſt com before God with the beſt preparation they can get. Hee will bee ſanctified in all them that draw nigh unto him. This the blinde Heathens ſaw, and therefore ſaid, (Plutarch.) [ilegible], worſhip not God by the by, but with all poſſible preparation. Hence they had their coena pura before their ſolemn ſacrifices. (Bucholcer.) Numa nihil rerum ſacrarum cives voluit neglectim agere. Hinc ſolenne illud, Hoc agite. The Miniſters likewiſe in the Primitive Church prepared the people's mindes by ſaying, Surſum corda, Lift up your hearts; (Cyprian. de Oratione. Chryſoſt. Baſil.) and the Deacons uſed to call upon the people in theſe words, Oremus, attendamus: Let us praie, let us attend.

entries.title: Exodus 19:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Againſt the third daie] That is, three daies hence, on the daie of Pentecoſt.

entries.title: Exodus 19:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That yee go not up into the Mount] God love's at once familiaritie and fear (ſaith a learned Divine) familiaritie with him in our converſation, (D. Hall.) and fear of him in his commands. Hee love's to bee acquainted with men in the walks of their obedience, yet hee take's ſtate upon him in his ordinances and will bee trembled at in his Word and Judgments.

entries.title: Exodus 19:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They ſhall com up to the Mount] i. e. To the bottom of the Mount, to the foot thereof. Verſ 17. See the Note on Heb. 12.20.

entries.title: Exodus 19:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And waſhed their clothes] In token of waſhing their hearts, and cleanſing themſelvs from all filthineſs of fleſh and ſpirit. The Gentiles alſo waſhed, (Plaut. in Alul. Act. 3. ſcen. 6. Tertul. cap. 11. de Orat.) that they might go to ſacrifice: and the Primitive Chriſtians before Praier.

entries.title: Exodus 19:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bee readie againſt the third daie] If the word of a Command exſpected ſuch readineſs, what ſhall the word of Promiſs? &c. [Com not at your wives] For the Legal uncleanneſs that was in it. Lev. 15.18. 1 Sam. 21.4. figuring the filth of original ſin.

entries.title: Exodus 19:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There were thunders and lightnings] The Law was delivered in this terrible manner; partly to procure reverence to the Doctrine of it, and partly to ſet forth the Nature and Office of it; which is to terrifie and thunder-ſtrike offenders.

entries.title: Exodus 19:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To meet with God] Who came with ten thouſands of his Saints, as Moſes (that climbed up that hill, (Deut. 33.2.) and alone ſaw it) ſaie's. And if hee thus gave the Law, how ſhall hee require it at the laſt daie?

entries.title: Exodus 19:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Lord deſcended upon it in fire] This fire wherein the Law was given, is ſtill in it, and will never out. Deut. 33.2.

entries.title: Exodus 19:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Moſes ſpake] Yet not without horror. Heb. 12.21.

entries.title: Exodus 19:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes went up] As a Mediator between God and his people. Gal. 3.19. with Acts 7.38. A Mediator Moſes was, not of Redemption (as Chriſt that Mediator of the new Covenant and ſuretie of a better Teſtament. Heb. 7.22. and 9.15.) but of receiving the Law, and delivering it to the people, for which end here hee went up.

entries.title: Exodus 19:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And manie of them periſh] As the men of Bethſhemeſh did for prying into the Ark. 1 Sam. 6.19. Arcana Dei, ſunt Arca Dei: (Calvin.) God's ſecrets are his Ark. Eorum quae ſcire nec datur, nec fas eſt, docta eſt ignorantia; ſcientiae appetentia, inſaniae ſpecies. Not to know what is not fit to know, is a learned ignorance: to deſire to know in that caſe is a kinde of madneſs. Hee that curiouſly ſearcheth into God's Majeſtie, ſhall bee oppreſſed of his glorie.

entries.title: Exodus 19:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And let the Prieſts] The firſt-born of the familie, which before the Levitical Law, had the Prieſt-hood. [Sanctifie themſelvs] With a ſingular care, above that of the reſt of the people. Much is required of Miniſters.

entries.title: Exodus 19:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The people cannot com up] i. e. Siquid ego aut capio, aut ſapio, they cannot: that which I know not teach thou mee.

entries.title: Exodus 19:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Away, get thee down] Abundans cautela non nocet. It is fit that men ſhould know and keep their diſtance. [Thou and Aaron with thee] Theſe onely (who were types of Chriſt's Princely and Prieſtly office) might com up unto the Lord.

entries.title: Exodus 20:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ALL the Ten are of divine autoritie. Papiſts diſanulling the ſecond, that yet they may retein the number of ten words (ſo loth are Hereticks to have their aſſ[ilegible] cars ſeon) they divide the laſt, which yet is called the Commandement, not the Commandements. Rom. 7.7. Vaſques not able to anſwer our Argument, ſaith, That the ſecond Commandement belonged to the Jews onely.

entries.title: Exodus 20:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which have brought thee] God's bleſſings are binders; and everie deliverance a tie to obedience.

entries.title: Exodus 20:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt have] This Thou reacheth everie man. Xenophon ſaith of Cyrus, that when hee gave anie thing in command, hee never ſaid, Let ſom one do this; but, Do thou this. (Hoc tu facias. Xenophon. Cyropaed.) [No other Gods before mee] But know and ſerv mee alone with a perfect heart, and with a willing minde. 1 Chron. 28.9.
