Hoc primo praecepto reliquorum omnium obſervantia praecipitur, ſaith Luther. In this firſt Commandement the keeping of all the other nine is commanded.

entries.title: Exodus 20:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not make unto thee] i. e. For religious uſe; for civil they may bee made. Mat. 22.20. Howbeit the Turks will not indure anie Image, no not upon their coins, becauſ of this ſecond Commandement. The Papiſts by their ſacrilegeous practices have taken away this Commandement out of their vulgar Catechiſm. This is a great ſtumbling-block to the Jews, and a let to their converſion: for ever ſince their return from Babylon, they do infinitely abhor Idolatrie. And for their coming to Chriſtian Sermons, they ſaie, That as long as they ſhall ſee the Preacher direct his ſpeech and praier to that little wooden Crucifix, that ſtand's on the Pulpit by him, (Specul. Europ.) to call it his Lord and Saviour, to kneel to it, to embrace it, to kiſs it, to weep upon it (as is the faſhion of Italie) this is preaching ſufficient for them, and perſwade's them more with the verie ſight of it, to hate Chriſtian Religion, then anie reaſon that the world can allege to love it.

entries.title: Exodus 20:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not bow down] Images came firſt from Babylon. For Ninus having made an Image of his father Belus, all that came to ſee it were pardoned for their former offenſes: whence in time that Image came to bee worſhipped, through the inſtigation of the Divel, who is, ſaith Syneſius, [ilegible], one that rejoiceth in Images. [Am a jealous God] Bee the gods of the Heathens good-fellows, ſaith one: the true God is a jealous God and will not ſhare his glorie with another, nor bee ſerved by anie but in his own waie. They that wit-wanton it with God, may look to ſpeed worſ then that Citizen in K. Edward the Fourth's daies did; who was executed in Cheapſide as a traitor, (Speed's Chron) for ſaying hee would make his ſon heir of the crown; though hee onely meant his own houſ, having a crown for the ſign. [Viſiting the iniquitie] This ſecond Commandement is the firſt with puniſhment: becauſ men do commonly puniſh ſuch as worſhip God in ſpirit and truth. As therefore one fire, ſo one fear ſhould drive out another; the fear of God, the fear of men.

entries.title: Exodus 20:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋnto thouſands] Of ſucceeding generations. Perſonal goodneſs is profitable to poſteritie. And this promiſs though made to all, yet is more ſpecially annexed to this ſecond Commandement; to teach (ſaith one) that parents ſhould chiefly labor to plant pietie in their families, as they would have God's bleſſing intailed upon their iſſue.

entries.title: Exodus 20:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Name of the Lord] That holie and reverend Name. Pſal. 111.9. that Nomen Majeſtativum, as Tertullian calleth it, dreadful among the Heathen. Mal. 1.14. The verie Turks at this daie chaſtiſe the Chriſtians that live amongſt them for their oaths and blaſphemies, darted up againſt God and Chriſt. The Jews alſo are much offended thereat, and it ſhould bee no ſmall grief to us to hear it. When one of Darius his Eunuchs ſaw Alexander the Great ſetting his feet upon a low table that had been highly eſteemed by his maſter, hee wept. (Diod. Sic. lib. 17.) Beeing asked the reaſon by Alexander, hee ſaid, It was to ſee the thing that his maſter ſo highly eſteemed, to bee now contemned, and made his foot-ſtool.

entries.title: Exodus 20:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Remember the Sabbath daie] Hee ſaith not, The ſeventh daie from the Creätion, but the daie of religious reſt; ſuch as is now our Chriſtian Sabbath, called a Sabbath-daie by our Saviour. Mat. 24.20. who is Lord of this Sabbath; called therefore the Lord's-daie, (Rev. 1. 1 Cor. 10.) as one of our Sacraments is called the Lord's Supper, and the table of the Lord, becauſ inſtituted by him. Pope Sylveſter preſumed to alter the Chriſtian Sabbath; (Hoſpin. de feſt Chriſt.) decreeing that Thurſdaie ſhould bee kept through the whole year; becauſ on that daie Chriſt aſſcended, and on that inſtituted the bleſſed Sacrament of his bodie and bloud. And generally Papiſts preſs the ſanctification of the Sabbath as a mere humane inſtitution in religious worſhip; an ordinance of the Church; and do in their celebration more ſolemnly obſerv the Feſtivals of the Saints, then the Lord's Sabbaths, making it as Bacchus's Orgies, &c. that, according to what their practice is, it may more fitly bee ſtyled, Dies daemoniacus quàm Dominicus. The divel's-daie then God's. [To ſanctifie it] Let everie one of us keep the Sabbath ſpiritually, (ſaith Ignatius) [ilegible], (Epiſt. 3.2d Magneſian.) rejoicing in the meditation of Chriſt's Law, more then in the reſt of our bodies. The ox and aſs muſt reſt, wee muſt conſecrate a reſt: [ilegible]s God on the ſeventh daie reſted not from his works of preſervation. John 5.17.

entries.title: Exodus 20:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Six daies ſhalt thou labor] God hath reſerved but one daie in ſeven, (as hee reſerved the Tree of knowledg of Good and Evil. Gen. 2.) yet wretched men muſt needs clip the Lord's coin. In manie places God's Sabbaths are made the voider and dunghil for all refuſe buſineſſes. The Sabbath of the Lord, the ſanctified day of his reſt (ſaith one) is ſhameleſly troubled and diſquieted. (B. King on Jon. Lect. 7.) The world is now grown perfectly profane (ſaith another) and can plaie on the Lord's-daie without book.

entries.title: Exodus 20:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But the ſeventh daie] Or, a ſeventh daie. Not onely Hebrews, but alſo Greeks and Barbarians, did reſt from work on the ſeventh daie: witneſs Joſephus, Clemens Alexand. and Euſehius. That which they tell us of the river Sabbatius it's reſting, and not running on that daie, I look upon as fabulous. [Thou ſhalt not do anie work] Onely works of Pietie, of Charitie, and of Neceſſitie may bee don on the Sabbath daie. Hee that but gathered ſticks was paid home with ſtones. The firſt blow given the Germane Churches was upon the Sabbath daie, (Dike of Conſ. pag. 276.) which they careleſly obſerved. Prague was loſt upon that daie. [Thou and thy ſon, &c.] Everie mother's childe. The baſer ſort of people in Swethland do alwaies break the Sabbath, (David's deſire by. R. Abbot.) ſaying, That it's for Gentlemen to keep that daie. [Thy manſervant] There is an old law of the Saxon King Ina, If a villain work on Sundaie by his Lord's command, hee ſhall bee free. (Sr. H Spelman in Concil.)

entries.title: Exodus 20:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For in ſix daies] God took ſix daies to make the world in, to the end, that wee might bee in a muſe when wee think of it; and think on his works in that order that hee made them. [And reſted the ſeventh daie] Not as tired out, (for hee made all without either tool or toil; his Fiat onely did the deed) but to give us example, as John 13.15. [Wherefore the Lord bleſſed, &c.] How God eſteemeth the ſtrict obſervation of the Sabbath daie, may appear by the exact deliverie of it. For hee hath fenced it about, like Mount Sinai, with marks and bounds, that profaneneſs might not approach it. 1. By his watch-word, Remember. 2. By his bountie, Six daies, &c. 3. By his ſovereigntie, It is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God. 4. By the latitude, Thou and thy ſon, &c. 5. By his own example, And reſted the ſeventh daie. 6. By his benediction, as here, Hee bleſſed it, and ordained it to bee a means of much bleſſing to thoſe that obſerv it. Add hereunto, that God hath placed this Command in the midſt of the Decalogue, betwixt the two tables; as much conducing to the keeping of both. It ſtand's like the ſenſus communis between the inward and outward ſenſes, (Bo[ilegible]in. Theat. Naturae.) beeing ſerviceable to both. [And hallowed it] Diem ſeptimam opifex, ut mundi natalem, ſibi ſacravit.

entries.title: Exodus 20:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Honor thy father, &c.] Philo well obſerveth, that this fifth Commandement (which therefore hee maketh a branch of the firſt Table, and ſo divide's the Tables equally) is a mixt Commandement; ([ilegible].) and differ's ſomwhat from the reſt of thoſe in the ſecond Table. They conſider man as our neighbor, in nature like us: this, as God's Deputie by him ſet over us, and in his name, and by his autoritie performing offices about us. [That thy daies may bee long] A good childe lengthneth his father's daies; therefore God promiſeth to lengthen his. Ill children, as they bring their parents graie hairs with ſorrow to the grave; ſo they are manie times cut off in the midſt of their daies, as Abimelech was: God rendring upon him the evil that hee did to his father. Judg. 13.5. Beſides the pnniſhment they have in their poſteritie (to whom they have been peremptores potiùs quàm parentes.) (Bern.) One complained that never father had ſo undutiful a childe as hee had: yes, ſaid his ſon, (with leſs grace then truth) my grandfather had.

entries.title: Exodus 20:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not kill] A crying ſin. Gen. 4. For the which God make's inquiſition. Pſalm 9.12. and ſtrangely bring's it to light. It was a ſaying of King James, that if God did leav him to kill a man, hee would think God did not love him.

entries.title: Exodus 20:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not commit adulterie] Adulterie onely is named; becauſe beſtialitie, Sodomie, and other uncleanneſſes (though more hainous) yet they do not directly fight againſt the puritie of poſteritie, and humane ſocietie, which the Law mainly reſpect's.

entries.title: Exodus 20:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not ſteal] i.e. Not rob or wrong another, ([ilegible]. Naz.) either by force or fraud. 1 Theſ. 4.6. See the Note there. Baſil chargeth the Divel as a thief of the truth, in that hee had decked his crows with her feathers. And it was of the Divel ſurely that Shee had learned her anſwer, who beeing charged by her miſtreſs for ſtealing her linnens, (Light for ſmoke. p. 85.) and other things which ſhee found in her trunk, ſaid, that ſhee ſtole them not: and when ſhee was asked, how came they to bee laid and locked up there? Did not you do this? No (ſaid ſhee) it was not I, but ſin that dwelleth in mee.

entries.title: Exodus 20:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not bear] Neither bear it, nor hear it; raiſ, nor receiv wrong reports of another. Deut. 19.16. Make a lie, nor love it when it is made. Rev. 22.15. The truth muſt bee ſpoken, and that in love. Doeg had a falſ tongue, though hee ſpoke nothing but truth againſt David. Pſal. 120.3.

entries.title: Exodus 20:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Thou ſhalt not covet] See the Note on Rom. 7.7. and on Heb. 13.5. [Thy neighbor's houſ] Houſe is here firſt ſet, as that which hold's and harbor's all the reſt.

To theſe ten words written by God himſelf in the daie of the Aſſemblie, Divines have reduced thoſe other Laws, Moral, Judicial, and Cerimonial, written by Moſes. 34.27, 28. Deut. 10.4. And herein Alſtedius (that excellent Methodiſt) hath in his Harmonia Muſica (as in all thoſe brief but pithie Notes upon the Pentateuch) don the Church of Chriſt ſingular good ſervice; whom therefore (for a Preface to that which follow's in the opening of this and the three next Books, and for the uſe of mine Engliſh Reader) I have abbridged, tranſlated, and the ſame here inſerted.

entries.title: Exodus 21:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THe Judicial Laws, fitly annexed to the Decalogue, whereof the Civil Magiſtrate is the Lord-keeper. It was written upon the ſword of Charls the Great, Decem praeceptorum cuſtos Carolus.

entries.title: Exodus 21:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In the ſeventh year] No longer might they ſerv, becauſ they were God's ſervants. Lev. 25.25. whoſe privilege ſee Iſa. 65.13, 14. Chriſt's free-men. (1 Cor. 2.27.)

entries.title: Exodus 21:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: If hee com in by himſelf] without a ſecond-ſelf, a yoke-fellow, ſtanding on even-ground with himſelf, though drawing on the left ſide.

entries.title: Exodus 21:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Have given him a wife] viz. One of his Heathen hand-maids, whom to part with was no great puniſhment, becauſ an unlawful couple.

entries.title: Exodus 21:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I love my maſter] A little better then hee in Plautus that ſaid, Ego non ſervio libenter; herus meus me non habet libenter, tamen utitur me ut lippis oculis.

entries.title: Exodus 21:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And ſhee ſhall ſerv him] Beeing [ilegible], as Ariſtotle hath it, the maſter's inſtrument, underling, and wholly his. Hee doth his own and not his maſter's will, that doth no more then himſelf will: this is a holiedaie ſervant as they ſaie.

entries.title: Exodus 21:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shee ſhall not go out] But upon better terms. Hee that was to come in the ſhape of a ſervant, ([ilegible]il. 2.) ſee what care hee take's of poor ſervant's welfare. Lawyers ſeldom ſpeak but for great men, or when they may have great gifts. Chriſt is not of that humor.

entries.title: Exodus 21:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee hath dealt deceitfully with her] By not anſwering her expectation. This God tolerated for the hardneſs of their hearts, but approved not.

entries.title: Exodus 21:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: After the manner of daughters] Not put her off (as they ſaie they do their daughters in Hungarie) without a portion, onely with a new coat at their wedding: much leſs, ſet her to ſale as the Thracians did their young brides; Quae non moribus nubebant ſed praemiis. (Solin. cap. 15.)

entries.title: Exodus 21:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Her dutie of marriage] See 1 Cor. 7. with the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 21:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And if hee do not anie of theſe three] Picus eſt imago ingrati mariti, (Me anththon.) quia ſub autumnum ejicit conjugem nè cogatur per hyemem nutrire: postea ſub vernum tempus eam ad ſe blandè revocat, ac in conſortium recipit.

entries.title: Exodus 21:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall bee ſurely put to death] See the Note on Gen. 9.6.

entries.title: Exodus 21:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But God deliver him] Who is the Lord of our lives, and to whom wee have frequently forfeited them; ſo that it is his mercie that wee are not conſumed. Lam. 3. That wee are not cut off from the land of the living.

entries.title: Exodus 21:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt take him, &c. A man that doth violence to the blood of anie perſon ſhall flee to the pit, let none ſtaie him. Pro. 28.17. Where the word Adam rendered Man hath in the original a little d: to ſhew that a murtherer is not worthie to bee called a man; hee is to bee drawn from the Altar to the ſlaughter.

entries.title: Exodus 21:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee that ſmiteth] By the law of God, of Nature, and of Nations, ſuch a man ſhould die. And herein, I think our laws are defective: albeit, I am not of Caroloſtadius his minde, who (if Melanchthon miſreport him not) held, that theſe Judicial Laws ſet down by Moſes ſhould bee ſtill of force (and theſe onely) in Chriſtian Common-wealths, and all other Civil and Municipal Laws aboliſhed.

entries.title: Exodus 21:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee that ſtealeth a man] A kin to theſe are they that ſteal other men's books, and father them; ſetting them out in their own names. Diagoras was ſo ſerved by a Plagiarie, which when hee ſaw, and that the thief was not preſently ſtruck with a thunder-bolt, hee out of ſtomach turned Atheïſt. Thus of late Fabricius ſtole Tremelius his Syriack Tranſlation. Villavincentius ſtole Hyperius his Treatiſ De ratione ſtudii Theologici. And Poſſevinus ſtole Dr. James his Cyprianus redivivus.

entries.title: Exodus 21:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And hee that curſeth] See the Note on Verſ 15. and on Mat. 15.4.

entries.title: Exodus 21:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: If men ſtrive together] This is counted man-hood, when indeed it is dog-hood rather: Heathens condemned it, (Immane verbum eſt ultio. Seneca Qui ulciſcitu[ilegible], excuſatiùs peccat. Sen.) and yet Navarrus a Popiſh Calviſt, Caedem rectè admitti putat, ut alapa vitetur, & ad honorem recuperandum.

entries.title: Exodus 21:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee ſhall bee ſurely puniſhed] At the diſcretion of the Magiſtrate, who is the revenger to execute wrath upon him that doth evil. Rom. 13.4.

entries.title: Exodus 21:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For hee is his monie] And therefore hee hath power over his fleſh. Col. 3.22. Yet hide not thine eies from thine own fleſh, ſaith the Prophet. (Iſa. 58.7.)

entries.title: Exodus 21:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And no miſchief follow] i. e. No life bee loſt. There is a time then, when the embryo is not alive; therefore the ſoul is not begotten, but infuſed after a time by God. Infundendo creatur, & creando infunditur, ſaith Aug. who at firſt doubted, till overcom by Hierom's arguments. (Auguſtin.)

entries.title: Exodus 21:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Eie for eie] How the Phariſees had wreſted that Text, See the Note on Mat. 5.39. This kinde of law (in uſe among Heathens alſo) Ariſtotle call's [ilegible], and was given againſt private revenge.

entries.title: Exodus 21:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Then the ox ſhall bee ſurely ſtoned] God requiring man's blood even of beaſts. Gen. 9.5. See the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 21:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee hath killed a man, &c.] Since the fall, all creatures are armed againſt us; as that ſword which Hector gave Ajax; which ſo long as hee uſed againſt men (his enemies) ſerved for help and defence: but after hee began to abuſe it to the hurt of hurtleſs beaſts, it turned into his own bowels.

entries.title: Exodus 21:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thirtie ſhekels] This ſame was that goodly price, that our Lord Chriſt was valued at by the vile Jews. Zach. 11.12, 13. Mat. 26.15.

entries.title: Exodus 21:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And an ox or an aſs] Wee can hardly open the deep pit of God's bottomleſs, boundleſs mercie, but ſom ſillie beaſt will bee falling thereinto; ſtumbling at the Word, beeing diſobedient, whereunto alſo they were appointed. 1 Pet. 2.8.

entries.title: Exodus 21:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ox for ox] Theſe where thoſe right judgments, true laws, good ſtatutes, &c. Neh. 9.13.

entries.title: Exodus 22:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THe Perſians at this daie puniſh theft and man-ſlaughter ſo ſeverely, (The Preachers Travels by Cartwright.) that in an age a man ſhall hardly hear either of the one or the other. The Turk's juſtice will rather cut off two innocent men, then let on thief eſcape.

entries.title: Exodus 22:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: If a thief bee found] So if an adultereſs bee taken, as ſhee was. John 8.4. [ilegible], in the verie theft.

entries.title: Exodus 22:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: If the ſun bee riſen] Chaldee hath it, If the eie of witneſſes: if hee can raiſ the town, and call in aid.

entries.title: Exodus 22:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee ſhall reſtore double] In Solomon's time it was ſeven-fold. Prov. 6.31.

entries.title: Exodus 22:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To bee eaten] By unadviſed turning in of his cattle, through miſtake or neglect.

entries.title: Exodus 22:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or the field] The ſtubble.

entries.title: Exodus 22:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or ſtuff] Heb. Veſſels, inſtruments, ornaments, apparel, furniture, weapons, &c.

entries.title: Exodus 22:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To ſee whether] ſc. by putting him to his oath Ver. 11. Som think that a private oath may bee in ſuch a caſe as this lawfully taken for the ſatisfaction of another, if hee will not otherwiſe bee ſatisfied.

entries.title: Exodus 22:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Before the Judges] Heb. the Gods: So Judges are called, if good eſpecially. Pſal. 82.6. And the ſeat of Judicature is called the holie place. Eccleſ. 8.10.

entries.title: Exodus 22:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or anie beaſt to keep] As Jacob kept Laban's cattle. Gen. 31.39.

entries.title: Exodus 22:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An oath of the Lord] Who is called in, as a witneſs and as an avenger: how hateful then is that Popiſh proverb and practiſe, Mercatorum eſt, non regum, ſtare juramentis?

entries.title: Exodus 22:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let him bring it] A leg, or a limb of it, as Amos 3.12.

entries.title: Exodus 22:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And if a man borrow] God hath ſo ordered humane condition that one man muſt bee beholden to another.

entries.title: Exodus 22:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It came for his hire] q. d. Hee ſhall paie the hire onely and no more, though the owner bee not by, when it miſcarrieth.

entries.title: Exodus 22:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Entice a maid] Heb. Over-perſwade with her, by fair words, which make fools fain.

entries.title: Exodus 22:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee ſhall paie] No mulct is laid upon her, becauſ ſhee had nothing of her own; and ſhee had loſt her honor, in loſing her virginitie. 1 Theſ. 4.4. See the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 22:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A witch] An enchantreſs, ſorcereſs, whoſe help was ſomtimes ſought, in inticing young maids to follie. The man-witch alſo is here meant, (Vatab.) but the woman-witch mentioned; both becauſ women are more inclinable to that ſin; and alſo becauſ the weaker ſex is not to bee ſpared for this fault. (Junius.)

entries.title: Exodus 22:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bee put to death] Heb. Put him to die. Gr. kill him with death, as God threatneth to do Jezabel's children. Rev. 2.23.

entries.title: Exodus 22:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee ſhall bee utterly deſtroied] As an execrable and accurſed creature.

entries.title: Exodus 22:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not vex a ſtranger] The right of ſtrangers is ſo holie (ſaith one) that there was never nation ſo barbarous that would violate the ſame. When Stephen Gardner had in his power the renowned Divine Peter Martyr, (Acts and Mon fol. 1783.) then teaching at Oxford, hee would not keep him to puniſh him; but when hee ſhould go his waie, gave him wherewith to bear his charges.

entries.title: Exodus 22:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or fatherleſs childe] With God the fatherleſs findeth mercie. Hoſ. 14.3. Widdows and orphans are God's clients taken into his protection.

entries.title: Exodus 22:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they crie at all unto mee] A vine, whoſe root is uncovered, thrive's not: ſo a widdow, whoſe covering of eies is taken away, (Mercer. in Proverb.) joie's not. In Hebrew ſhee is called Almanach of Alam to bee dumb; becauſ ſhee hath none to ſpeak for her. But if ſhee call and crie to God, hee will ſpeak for her in the hearts of her oppreſſors.

entries.title: Exodus 22:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Your wives ſhall bee widdows] God delight's to puniſh crueltie in kinde, as hee did in Agag. 1 Sam. 15.33.

entries.title: Exodus 22:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not bee to him as an uſurer] Heb. as an exacting creditor, Qui nullum diem gratìs occidere creditori permittit. The uſurer's monie is to neceſſitie, like cold water to a hot ague, that for a time refreſheth, but prolongeth the diſeaſ. [Laie upon him uſurie] Heb. Biting uſurie. Uſurers are men-eaters. Pſalm 14.4. Like pickrels in a pond, or ſharks in the ſea that devour the leſſer fiſhes. Theſe oſtriches can digeſt anie metal, eſpecially monie. (Ariſt. Ethic. lib. 4. cap. 1.) Ariſtotle in one page condemneth the uſurer and the dicer; and yet ſom Chriſtians bluſh at neither.

entries.title: Exodus 22:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not revile the Gods] Blaſpheme dignities. This is blaſphemie in the ſecond Table. (Jude 8.)

entries.title: Exodus 22:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not delaie] True obedience is prompt and preſent, readie and ſpeedie, without demur and conſults, Zech. 5.9. wings and winde in their wings. [On the eighth daie] When a Sabbath had once gon over it, ſaie the Hebrews.

entries.title: Exodus 22:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Holie men] Heb. Men of holineſs, which ſhould run through our whole lives, as the woof doth through the web.

entries.title: Exodus 23:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: NEither raiſ nor receiv it; neither bee the tale-bearer, nor tale-hearer: the one carrie's the divel in his tongue, the other in his ear. Not onely thoſe that make a lie, but thoſe that love it when it is made to their hands, are ſhut out of heaven. Rev. 22.15. Solomon make's it an ill ſign of a graceleſs man, to bee apt to beleev ſcandalous reports of godlie perſons. Prov. 17.4.

entries.title: Exodus 23:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not follow a multitude] The waie to hell is broad and well-beaten. Per viam publicam nè ingredere, was one of Pythagoras his precepts: Do not as the moſt do, leſt thou bee undon for ever. Argumentum turpiſſimum eſt turba, ſaith Seneca. To live according to the courſ of the world is to bee acted by the divel. Epheſ. 2.2.

entries.title: Exodus 23:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Neither ſhalt thou countenance] Spare not the great for their might, nor the mean for their miſerie.

entries.title: Exodus 23:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ox, or his aſs going aſtraie] How much more his ſoul? See the Notes on Jam. 5.20. Jude 22, 23.

entries.title: Exodus 23:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt ſurely help with him] So the Spirit help's with us; or liſt's over againſt us. Rom. 8.26. ([ilegible].) Hee look's ut acti agamus.

entries.title: Exodus 23:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The judgment of the poor] I have ſeen (ſaith one) the King of Perſia manie times to alight from his horſ, (The Preachers Travels by J. Cartwright.) onely to do juſtice to a poor bodie. Cauſſes are to bee heard and not perſons: the Athenian Judges paſſed ſentence in the dark.

entries.title: Exodus 23:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Keep thee from a falſ matter] Stand aloof of, keep at a diſtance. See Iſa. 33.15. A publike man ſhould bee above all price or ſale: and everie man ſhould carefully keep himſelf from the occaſions of ſin. A good man dare not com near the train, though hee bee far off the blow.

entries.title: Exodus 23:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And thou ſhalt take no gift] Rain is good, and ground is good; yet Ex eorum conjunctione fit lutum, ſaith Stapleton: So giving is kinde, and taking is courteous, yet the mixing of them make's the ſmooth paths of Juſtice foul and uneven.

entries.title: Exodus 23:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt not oppreſs, &c.] See the Note on Exod. 22.21.

entries.title: Exodus 23:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt ſow thy land] Here the wiſe man's counſel would bee remembered, Laudato ingentia rura, exiguum colito. To bee called a good husbandman, was of old an high praiſ.

entries.title: Exodus 23:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But the ſeventh year] That they might learn to live by faith, and bee at good leiſure to wait upon God. Deut. 31.10, 11, 12. Let everie of us keep a ſpiritual Sabbath, ſaith Ignatius, [ilegible], (Ep. 3. ad Magneſ.) Better apaid of the meditation of the Law, then of the relaxation and reſt from labor.

entries.title: Exodus 23:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Six daies] See the Note on Chap. 20.8.

entries.title: Exodus 23:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bee circumſpect] Or warie, keep you cloſe to the rule, and up to your principles. See the Note on Epheſ. 5.15. [Of the names of other Gods] ſc. Without diſlike. The Primitive Chriſtians would not call their daies of the week, Dies Martis, Mercurii, &c. as Mercurius Triſmegiſtus had named them; but the firſt, ſecond, third, &c. daie of the week, Deaſtrorum nomina nè nota quidem eſſe voluerunt inter Chriſti cultores, ſaith one. They deſired that Chriſtians ſhould ſpit out of their mouths thoſe dunghill-deïties with utmoſt contempt, as David did. Pſalm 16.4.

entries.title: Exodus 23:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt keep the feaſt] Let us alſo keep the feaſt, or Holie-daie. 1 Cor. 5.8. See the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 23:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the feaſt of harveſt] Pentecoſt, when their wheat-harveſt came in. [In the end of the year] See the reaſon of this law. Deut. 11.12. It was a land which the Lord cared for: the eies of the Lord were alwaies upon it from the begining of the year, even unto the end of the year.

entries.title: Exodus 23:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All thy males] The female are not required to appear, becauſ they were weak, and not ſo fit for travel: they were alſo the houſ-keepers, and ſanctified in their husbands. Howbeit manie of them came up to theſe feaſts, as Hannah. 1 Sam. 2.19. And the virgin Marie. Luke 2.41. And this was well accepted as a Free-will-offering.

entries.title: Exodus 23:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of my ſacrifice] Eſpecially of the Paſſover. See Exod. 34.25. Lev. 2.1, 2, 3.

entries.title: Exodus 23:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The firſt of the firſt-fruits] The beſt of the beſt is not to bee held too good for God. His ſoul hath deſired the firſt ripe fruits. Jer. 2.2. [Thou ſhalt not ſeeth a kid] Hereby ſeemeth to bee forbidden either crueltie, or curioſitie to pleaſ the palat. See my Common-place of Abſtinence.

entries.title: Exodus 23:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Behold, I ſend an Angel] i. e. Chriſt. Immediately after God had given the Law (by the rule and threats whereof God the Father in his government was to proceed, (Mr. Th. Goodwin.) ſaith a Divine) and after they had tranſgreſſed it. Exod. 33.2, 3, 4. hee could not go along with them, for hee ſhould deſtroie them: but his Angel, that is, his Son, hee would ſend with them; who alſo would deſtroie them, if they turned not, nor repented according to the rules of his Law, the Goſpel.

entries.title: Exodus 23:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: My name is in him] i. e. Hee is of the ſame nature with my ſelf. See Phil. 2.6. Heb. 1.3. with the Notes there.

entries.title: Exodus 23:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An enemie to thine enemies] There is a Covenant offenſive and defenſive betwixt God and his people. Tua cauſſa erit mea cauſſa, ſaid that Emperor to his wronged friend: So ſaith God to his.

entries.title: Exodus 23:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For mine Angel] Heb. Malachi, which is by tranſpoſition of letters Michael, as ſom Rabbins have obſerved.

entries.title: Exodus 23:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt utterly overthrow them] As Hen. 8. began here to do in demoliſhing the Monaſteries, and ſaying, Corvorum nidos eſſe penitùs diſturbandos nè iterùm ad habitandum convolent. This Sanders relateth and exagitateth. (Schiſm. Angl. lib. 1.)

entries.title: Exodus 23:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bleſs thy bread] God's bleſſing is the ſtaff of bread and ſtrength of water. See the Note on Mat. 4.4.

entries.title: Exodus 23:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The number of thy daies] Thou ſhalt die; as Abraham did, with a good hoar head: bee ſatur dierum as Job, fall as a full-ripe-apple into the hands of God the gatherer.

entries.title: Exodus 23:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: My fear before thee] Strike a panick fear into the hearts of thine enemies, ſo that they ſhall flee at the noiſ of a driven leaf, they ſhall bee made à corde ſuo fugitivi, as Tertullian hath it.

entries.title: Exodus 23:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hornets before thee] Underſtand it either literally as Joſh. 24.12. or figuratively, of the ſtinging terrors of their ſelf-condemning conſciences.

entries.title: Exodus 23:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In one year] God's time is beſt: and to preſcribe to him is to ſet the ſun by our dial. His help ſeem's long, becauſ wee are ſhort. Wait upon him, who wait's to ſhew us mercie. Iſa 30.18.

entries.title: Exodus 23:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By little and little] God crumble's his mercies to us; wee have his bleſſing by retail. So the cloud emptie's not it ſelf at a ſudden burſt, but diſſolv's upon the earth drop after drop.

entries.title: Exodus 23:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The ſea of the Philiſtims] i. e. the Mediterranean.

entries.title: Exodus 23:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: No covenant with them] becauſ devoted to deſtruction; and they will bee drawing thee to Idolarrie, as it alſo fell out, Judg. 1. & 2.

entries.title: Exodus 24:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THus under the Law, but now by grace wee draw nigh with boldneſs, and have acceſs with confidence by the faith of Chriſt. Epheſ. 3.12. See the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 24:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But they ſhall not com nigh] But half-waie onely. Verſ 19. See the Note on Chap. 19.12.

entries.title: Exodus 24:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And told the people] So hee became a Mediator. Gal. 3.19. Non redemptionis ſed relationis. [Will wee do] God's people are willing. Pſalm 110.3. But weak through the fleſh. Rom. 8.3. See the Note on Heb. 13.18.

entries.title: Exodus 24:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An Altar] Repreſenting God on the one partie, as the twelv pillars did the people on the other partie. So here was a formal covenant.

entries.title: Exodus 24:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Young men] The firſt-born of the families. Exod. 19.12.

entries.title: Exodus 24:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Half of the blood] Having mingled it firſt with water. Heb. 9.19. See 1 John 5.6. with the Note.

entries.title: Exodus 24:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Will wee do, and bee obedient] Chriſt will enjoie his ſpouſes love, by a willing contract, not by a raviſhment.

entries.title: Exodus 24:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: On the people] The repreſentative people, the elders: or, as others will, the twelv pillars. See Verſ 4.

entries.title: Exodus 24:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And ſeventie of the elders] See Verſ 2.

entries.title: Exodus 24:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they ſaw God] A glimpſ of his glorie. See the Note on 1 Tim. 6.16.

entries.title: Exodus 24:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Hee laid not his hand] i. e. They came off without hurt, which is reckoned as a great mercie: ſith no man (ordinarily) can ſee God and live: beſides the infinite diſtance that is betwixt God, and the greateſt Nobles. [And did eat and drink] i. e. They were much acheared and made merrie in the Lord. Others ſenſ it thus: Though they had ſeen God, yet they turned again to temporal pleaſures; they ſoon after ate & drunk at that idolatrous feaſt of the golden calf, and roſe up to plaie. It is ſet as an aggravation of Solomon's ſin that hee departed from God that appeared to unto him twice. 1 King. 11.9.

entries.title: Exodus 24:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Tables of ſtone] To ſhew 1. the ſtonie-hardneſs of the people's hearts. 2. The laſtingneſs of the Law.

entries.title: Exodus 24:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes went up] Joſhua ſtaid the while in ſom convenient place.

entries.title: Exodus 24:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Hur] See the Note on Chap. 17.10.

entries.title: Exodus 24:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Six daies] The people had but three daies of preparation to receiv the Law; Moſes hath ſix. Singular holineſs is required of Miniſters: the meaſures of the Sanctuarie were double to the ordinarie; as the ſhekel, cubit, &c. Miniſters had need wiſh, as Eliſha did, a doubled and trebled ſpirit, that they may ſave themſelvs, and thoſe that hear them.

entries.title: Exodus 24:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Was like devouring fire] So it is ſtill. Heb. 12.29. which ſo terriſieth the ſinners in Sion, that they run away with theſe words in their mouths, Who among us ſhall dwell with the devouring fire? Who amongſt us ſhall dwell with everlaſting burnings? Iſa. 33.14.

entries.title: Exodus 24:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Fortie daies] All which time hee neither ate nor drank. Deut. 9.9. and ſo better merited the ſirname of Neſteutes the Faſter, then that proud Prelate John Biſhop of Conſtantinople.

entries.title: Exodus 25:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: VIrtus nolentium nulla eſt; God ſtrain's upon no man. If yee conſent and obeie, &c. If there bee a willing minde, God accepteth, &c. 2 Cor. 8.11, 12.

entries.title: Exodus 25:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gold, and ſilver, and braſs] No mention of iron: Confer 1 King. 6.7. & 8.51.

entries.title: Exodus 25:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And blue, and purple, and ſcarlet] i. e. Wool died with theſe colors. Heb. 9.19. To teach the Church, that both themſelvs and their actions ſhould bee waſhed and died in the bloud of Chriſt.

entries.title: Exodus 25:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shittim wood] A kinde of cedar, that rotteth not. (Gal. lib. 1. Antidit.)

entries.title: Exodus 25:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Spices] As cinnamom, which in Galen's time was verie rare, and hard to bee found but in Prince's ſtore-houſes.

entries.title: Exodus 25:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That I may dwell amongſt them] But will God in verie deed dwell with men upon earth? (2 Chron. 6.18.) What can hee do more to make them happie? As hee in Plutarch ſaid of the Scythians, that although they had no muſick nor vines amongſt them, yet (as a better thing) they had Gods: and as the Philoſopher having little elſ in his houſ, yet could ſaie of it, [ilegible], Here bee Gods: ſo may everie good man boaſt of his houſ, and of his heart, (Heb. 3.6.2 Cor. 6.16. Gen. 28.17.) This is the habitation of the moſt High. As for the publick aſſemblie of Saints, This is the houſ of God, this is the gate of Heaven.

entries.title: Exodus 25:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An Ark] Cheſt, or Cabinet, wherein to keep the two Tables of the Law; ſignifying thereby that Chriſt is the end of the Law, covering the imperfection of our works.

entries.title: Exodus 25:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A crown of gold] To ſet forth the Majeſtie of Chriſt's kingdom, or the eternitie of his Deïtie; which, as a crown, or circle, had neither begining nor end.

entries.title: Exodus 25:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That the Ark may bee born with them] The Ark was tranſportative, till ſettled in Solomon's Temple: ſo till wee com to heaven ſhall wee bee in a continual motion:

entries.title: Exodus 25:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The ſtaves ſhall bee, &c.] That they might not touch it, for reverence ſake, it beeing a viſible ſign of God himſelf amongſt them.

entries.title: Exodus 25:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Teſtimonie] Thoſe tables of the Teſtimonie. Exod. 31.18. That teſtified what God required of them; and would bee a teſtimonie againſt them, if diſobedient. Deut. 31.26.

entries.title: Exodus 25:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Mercie-ſeat] Heb. A Covering, or coffering up of men's ſins, the appeaſing of an angrie God. (Confer Gen. 38.20.) By Chriſt who is our propitiation or Mercie-ſeat. Rom 3.25.1 John 2.2. [Two cubits and a half, &c.] Juſt ſo big everie waie as the Ark. Verſ 10. Get into Covenant with God (ſaith one) for as the Mercie-ſeat was no larger then the Ark, ſo neither is the grace of God then the Covenant. And as the Ark and Mercie-ſeat were not aſunder; ſo God is near to all that call upon him in truth.

entries.title: Exodus 25:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And thou ſhalt make two Cherubims] Golden winged images, made by God's ſpecial appointment, and ſet out of ſight: Hence then is no warrant for the uſe of images in Churches. Theſe here were to repreſent the holie Angels attendent upon God, looking intently into the myſterie of Chriſt, as the Cherubims did into the Propitiatorie. 1 Pet. 1.12. and joined to the ſocietie of Saints.

entries.title: Exodus 25:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Even of the Mercie-ſeat] Of the matter of it: to ſhew that the verie Angels have their eſtabliſhment in, and by Chriſt: and that, if they need mereie, how much more do wee? Angels alſo are under Chriſt as a head of Government, of Influence, of Confirmation, though not of Redemption.

entries.title: Exodus 25:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Toward the Mercie-ſeat ſhall the faces, &c.] Angels in the Syriack are called [ilegible] of the face; becauſ they look ever on the face of God, waiting his commands.

entries.title: Exodus 25:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Above upon the Ark] The Ark covering the Law within it, the Mercie-ſeat upon it, and over them two Cherubims covering one another, did typifie Chriſt covering the curſes of the Law, in whom is the ground of all Mercie; which things the Angels deſire to prie into, as into the pattern of God's deep wiſdoms.

entries.title: Exodus 25:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: From between the two Cherubims] which covered the place from whence the Lord ſpake, to reſtrain curioſitie.

entries.title: Exodus 25:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of Shittim wood] Which corrupteth not. Iſa. 41.19. Chriſt's bodie could not putrefie in the grave.

entries.title: Exodus 25:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Pure gold] Pointing to the glorie of Chriſt's Deïtie, and the Majeſtie of his Kingdom.

entries.title: Exodus 25:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A golden crown] To hide the joints, and for ornament. Chriſt alſo is ſaid to have manie crowns. Rev. 19.12.

entries.title: Exodus 25:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shew-bread] See the Note on Mat. 12.4.

entries.title: Exodus 25:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And thou ſhalt make a candleſtick] called the candleſtick of light. Exod. 35.14. A Type of Chriſt, who is [ilegible] light eſſential, and giveth light to everie man that cometh into the world. John 1.9. See the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 25:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Seven lamps] Signifying the manifold graces and diverſitie of gifts in the Church. Zech. 4.2.

entries.title: Exodus 25:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the tongs] All of gold; betokening the puritie of Doctrine and Diſcipline in the Church.

entries.title: Exodus 26:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
AType of Chriſt who dwelt among us, full of Graces and Truth. John 1.14.2. Of the Church built by Chriſt. 1 Cor. 3.9.3. Of everie true Chriſtian. Epheſ. 2.10.

Ver. [ilegible]. Shall bee coupled together] Theſe curtains were coupled with loops, ſo ſhould Chriſtians by love. My dove is but one: the daughters ſaw her and bleſſed her. Cant. 6.9. See Epheſ. 2.21, 22. & 4.16.

entries.title: Exodus 26:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With the taches] So is the unitie of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Epheſ. 4.3. [Shall bee one Tabernacle] See thoſe manie Ones. Epheſ. 4.3, 4, 5. with the Notes there.

entries.title: Exodus 26:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of goat's-half] The Tabernacle was goat's hair without, and gold within. God hid his Son under the Carpenter's ſon: The King's daughter is all glorious within. Pſalm 45.13. And all her ſons are Princes in all lands. Verſ 16. Howbeit they muſt bee content to paſs to heaven as Chriſt their Head did, as concealed men. Therefore the world know's us not, becauſ it knew not him. John 3.1. Our life is hid with Chriſt, Col. 3.4. as the life of flowers in winter is hid in the root.

entries.title: Exodus 26:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A covering for the tent] Shadowing out God's protecting his people. Iſa. 4.6. and 25.4. Pſalm 27.5. as theſe ram's-skins covered the Ark from the violence of winde and weather.

entries.title: Exodus 26:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With Cherubims] To note the ſpecial preſence and attendence of the holie Angels in the aſſemblies of the Saints. Luke 1.11. John 1.51.

entries.title: Exodus 26:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An hanging for the door] This ſhadowed him that ſaid of himſelf, I am the door. The Cerimonial Law was the Jews Goſpel, for it was Chriſt in figure; and to him it led them.

entries.title: Exodus 27:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SOlomon's Altar was four times as big as this: to teach, that as our peace and proſperitie is more then others, ſo ſhould our ſervice in a due proportion.

entries.title: Exodus 27:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Horns of it] To binde the beaſts unto that were to bee ſlain in ſacrifice. Pſalm 118.27. And to ſignifie the power of Chriſt's Prieſt-hood. Hab. 3.4. [Thou ſhalt over-laie it with braſs] The braſs kept the wood, ſo did the Deïtie of Chriſt keep his humanitie from beeing conſumed by the fire of God's wrath, wherein it was roſted.

entries.title: Exodus 27:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: His ſhovels and his baſins.] Theſe ſeveral inſtruments figured the Miniſterie of the word, ſaie ſom; the ſundrie callings that Chriſt hath in his Church, ſaie others, for her edification.

entries.title: Exodus 27:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A. grate] which ſerved for an hearth, and repreſented Chriſt, bearing the fire of his Father's diſpleaſure.

entries.title: Exodus 27:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the ſtaves ſhall bee] As ever readie to remove. Here wee have no aſſured ſettlement.

entries.title: Exodus 27:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The court of the Tabernacle] This outer court ſignified the viſible Church; where hypocrites alſo com to the external worſhips. Doeg may ſet his foot as far as David.

entries.title: Exodus 27:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the twentie pillars] In alluſion whereunto, the Church is called the pillar and ſtaie of truth. 1 Tim. 3.15.

entries.title: Exodus 27:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Pure oil olive] Signifying the pretious gifts and graces of the Spirit in godlie Miniſters, whoſe lips muſt both preſerv knowledg, and preſent it to the people.

entries.title: Exodus 28:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: CHriſt alſo was taken from amongſt men. Heb. 5.1. to mediate and negotiate man's cauſ with God: And this honor hee aſſumed not up to himſelf, but it was given him from above. Verſ. 5.

entries.title: Exodus 28:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For glorie and for beautie] Prodit Aäron à capite ad calcem, os humeróſque Deo ſimilis. The High-prieſt was gloriouſly apparelled, to ſtrike a religious reverence into the eies and hearts of the beholders; and to ſet forth the beautie and braverie of Chriſt and his Church.

entries.title: Exodus 28:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That they may make, &c.] Vides, in Sacerdotibus nîl plebeium reperiri, nîl populare, ſaith Ambroſe. Nothing in the Prieſts but what was above the ordinarie. The verie work-men are to bee filled with the Spirit of Wiſdom, to make their attire.

entries.title: Exodus 28:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they ſhall take gold and blue, &c.] That cloke of Alciſthenes the Sybarite (ſold for 1 20. talents) that Parliament-robe of Demetrius King of Macedonie, (Athenaeus.) (which no Prince after him would put on propter invidioſam impendii magnificentiam, ſot it's ſtately coſtlineſs) were but rags to Aaron's raiment.

entries.title: Exodus 28:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The ephod of gold] This the High-prieſt onely might wear, neither might anie imitate it; for that was the fall of Gideon's houſ. Judg. 8.26, 27.

entries.title: Exodus 28:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Aaron ſhall bear their names] To ſet forth Chriſt's unceſſant interceſſion for all God's Iſraël, even when his back ſeem's turned upon them.

entries.title: Exodus 28:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Faſten the wreathen chains] Theſe chains wherewith the breaſt-plate and humeral were tied, (Moſes unvail.) ſignified (ſaith one) the perfect contexture of all heavenlie virtues, adorning Chriſt's humanitie: as alſo that true ſaith, whereby wee are girt unto him.

entries.title: Exodus 28:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The breast plate of judgment] So called, becauſ the Prieſt was to put it on, when hee was to enquire and give ſentence as from God. Num. 27.21.

entries.title: Exodus 28:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Four rows of ſtones] According to the number and order of the twelv Tribes encamping about God's Tabernacle. In all which rows, (Dr. Tailor.) a verie Reverend Writer hath well obſerved eight things: 1. The ſhining of the ſtones; pointing to the puritie of Chriſt and his Church. 2. Their price; of great value and worth: ſignifying what a price Chriſt valued his Church at. 3. Their place or ſituation; they are ſet in the pectoral, and Aaron muſt carrie them on his heart, ſignifying that Chriſt hath as much care of his Church, as if it were incloſed in his heart; let's out his blood to make room in his heart for them. 4. Their number; twelv; noting, that with Chriſt is plentiful redemption. 5. Their order; they ſtood in a comlie quadrangle. Chriſt hath ſtabliſhed a comlie order in his Church; and wee muſt keep our ranks. 6. The figure; the four-ſquare; ſignifying the ſtabilitie and firmneſs of the Church. Satan and all deceivers ſhall not pick one ſtone out of Chriſt's pectoral. Their uſe; that Aaron muſt bear them on his heart; ſignifying Chriſt's ardent affection to his, and conſtant interceſſion for them. 8. The quantitie: As all the names of Iſraël were gathered into a narrow compaſs; ſo Chriſt ſhall gather together into one all the diſperſed ſons of God, and preſent them before God as the moſt beautiful and pretious parts of the world. John 11.52.

entries.title: Exodus 28:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Ʋrim and the Thummim] A diſtinct thing from the ſtones and chains; made it was not by the Artificers, but given by God to Moſes (as were the two Tables) and by him put into the breaſt-plate. The verie names of Ʋrim and Thummim, i. e. Lights and perfections lead us to Chriſt, in whom is all fulneſs. [When hee goeth in before the Lord] ſc. to conſult with God, who anſwered the Prieſt by voice. Num. 7.89.

entries.title: Exodus 28:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The robe of the ephod] Which ſignified the roial robe of Chriſt's righteouſneſs, reaching down to the feet, large enough to cover all our imperfections.

entries.title: Exodus 28:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That it bee not rent] To ſhew that there ſhould bee no rents or ſchiſms in the Church. 1 Cor. 1.10, 13.1 Tim. 1.3.

entries.title: Exodus 28:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A golden bell, and a pomegranate] Shadowing out 1. The Prophetical office of Chriſt here, and his perpetual interceſſion in heaven. 2. The dutie of Miniſters; which is, Vivere concionibus, concionari moribus: to live ſermons, to bee fruitful as well as painful teachers: Not like him of whom it was ſaid, that when hee was out of the pulpit, it was pitie hee ſhould ever go into it: and when hee was in the pulpit, it was pitie hee ſhould ever com out of it.

entries.title: Exodus 28:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And his ſound ſhall bee heard] Neceſſe erat ut Pontifex totus vocalis ingrederetur ſanctuarium, nè fortè non audito ſonitu, morte lueret ſilentium. A dumb dog is a childe of death. Iſa. 56.10. Miniſters muſt bee both able and apt to teach upon all occaſions.

entries.title: Exodus 28:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Holineſs to the Lord] Hence it was not lawful for the High-prieſt (ſaie the Jews) to put off his bonnet to whomſoever hee met, were hee never ſo great a man; leſt the Name and Glorie of God (whoſe perſon hee ſuſteined) ſhould ſeem to ſubmit to anie man.

entries.title: Exodus 28:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋpon the mitre] Which had an holie crown with it. Chap. 29.6. ſignifying the Deïtie and Dignitie of Chriſt.

entries.title: Exodus 28:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The iniquitie of the holie things] Get the people's pardon. This Chriſt did indeed for all his. 1 John 2.1, 2.

entries.title: Exodus 28:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Embroider the coat] Rev. 1.13. Chriſt is clothed with ſuch a robe, as King and Counſellor of his Church.

entries.title: Exodus 28:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Coats] Linnen garments for innocencie. 2. Girdles for conſtancie and ſtabilitie. 3. Bonnets, for ſafetie from the rage of Satan and his inſtruments. 4. Breeches, for comlie reverence in God's ſervice.

entries.title: Exodus 29:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: ALL ſorts of Sacrifices (Sin-offerings, Burnt-offerings, Peace-offerings) were to bee offered for the Prieſts, becauſ of the ſpecial holineſs and honor of their calling.

entries.title: Exodus 29:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And unleavened bread] See 1 Cor. 5.7, 8. with the Notes there.

entries.title: Exodus 29:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Waſh them with water] A type of Chriſt's Baptiſm, Matth. 3.

entries.title: Exodus 29:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The holie crown] See the Note on Chap. 28.37.

entries.title: Exodus 29:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The annointing oil] Typing out that abundance of the holie Spirit powred upon Chriſt. Iſa. 61.1. and upon Chriſtians. 1 John 2.27. Pſalm. 133.2.

entries.title: Exodus 29:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Coats, &c.] See the Note on Chap. 28.40.

entries.title: Exodus 29:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Conſecrate] Heb. Fill their hands, ſe. with ſacrifices: they were not to fill their own hands, as Jeroboam's Prieſts did. 1 King. 13.31. See Heb. 5.5.

entries.title: Exodus 29:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall put their hands] As transferring the guilt of their ſins upon Chriſt. Iſa. 53.6.

entries.title: Exodus 29:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By the door] Pointing to Chriſt, the door into heaven. Heb. 10.20.

entries.title: Exodus 29:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The blood of the bullock] For without blood, there was no remiſſion of ſin. [Beſide the bottom of the Altar] To ſignifie the plenteous Redemption wrought by Chriſt.

entries.title: Exodus 29:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All the fat that covereth] God muſt have the verie beſt of the beſt; ſith Chriſt offered himſelf, and the beſt parts hee had.

entries.title: Exodus 29:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Without the camp] See the Note on Heb. 13.12. and on Heb. 7.27, 28.

entries.title: Exodus 29:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt alſo take] After the Sin-offering, other offerings: till ſin bee expiated, no ſervice is accepted.

entries.title: Exodus 29:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sprinkle it] See 1 Pet. 1.2.

entries.title: Exodus 29:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Waſh the inwards of him] This ſignified that intire holineſs, that through ſanctification. 1 Theſ. 5.23.

entries.title: Exodus 29:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The whole ram] Rom. 1.1. with the Note.

entries.title: Exodus 29:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Put their hands] Both their hands between the horns of the ram.

entries.title: Exodus 29:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋpon the tip of the right ear] To ſet forth the holie obedience required of them in all their ſenſes, actions and motions. Iohn 13.5, 6, 9.

entries.title: Exodus 29:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of the blood, and of the annointing oil] Signifying Chriſt's Merit and Spirit.

entries.title: Exodus 29:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A ram of the conſecration] A Thank-offering to God for advancing Aaron to the Prieſt-hood. See the like in S. Paul. 1 Tim. 1.12.

entries.title: Exodus 29:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋnleavened bread] See 1 Cor. 5, 7, 8. with the Notes there.

entries.title: Exodus 29:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And ſhalt wave them] As acknowledging God's Omnipreſence: and that manie ſhould com from Eaſt, Weſt, North, and South, to partake of the Merits & Benefits of Chriſt, our true ſacrifice.

entries.title: Exodus 29:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is an offering made by fire] Chriſt in like ſort having offered himſelf for a Burnt-offering, for a ſweet ſavor before the Lord, aſſcended up into heaven, and gave gifts unto men.

entries.title: Exodus 29:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It ſhall bee thy part] Becauſ hee did for this time extraordinarily execute the Prieſt's office.

entries.title: Exodus 29:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The breaſt of the Wave-offering and ſhoulder] To teach the Prieſts to ſerv the Lord with all their hearts, and with all their ſtrength.

entries.title: Exodus 29:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Heav-offering] Signifying the heaving of Chriſt upon the Croſs, and the heaving up of our hearts to God for ſo great benefits.

entries.title: Exodus 29:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall bee his ſons after him] His garments remained for ever, ſo doth the robe of Chriſt's righteouſneſs. Iſa. 61.10.

entries.title: Exodus 29:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And that ſon] There were garments but for one: there is but one Mediator, the Man Chriſt Jeſus.

entries.title: Exodus 29:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And thou ſhalt take the ram] i. e. The remnant of him.

entries.title: Exodus 29:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And they ſhall eat thoſe things] Applie Chriſt's death by faith to their own ſouls. John 6.51.

entries.title: Exodus 29:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt burn the remainder] The Thank-offering was not to bee kept till the morrow, to teach us to bee prompt and preſent in praiſing God, and applying Chriſt.

entries.title: Exodus 29:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Seven daies] To teach the Prieſt's to conſecrate their whole lives to God's ſervice.

entries.title: Exodus 29:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Cleanſ the Altar] Which as well as the creatures, may bee defiled by man's ſin. Lev. 16.16.

entries.title: Exodus 29:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Whatſoever toucheth the Altar] See Matth. 23.19. with the Note there.

entries.title: Exodus 29:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Daie by daie continually] When this dailie ſacrifice was intermitted (as in the daies of Antiochus that little Anti-Chriſt) they counted it an abomination of deſolation.

entries.title: Exodus 29:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thou ſhalt offer in the morning] Theſe two lambs were types of the Lamb of God, taking away the ſins of the world, with a commemoration of whoſe benefits the daie was begun and ended. Wherefore, alſo from David's daies, and forwards, they ſang the 22 Pſalm at the Morning Sacrifice, and the 136 Pſalm at the Evening.

entries.title: Exodus 29:45
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And I will dwell] See the Note on 2 Cor. 6.16.

entries.title: Exodus 30:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SHadowing Chriſt, as perfuming and preſenting the Praiers of Saints. Rev. 8.3. and 5.8. and obteining anſwer thereto from the four horns of the golden Altar. Rev. 9.13.

entries.title: Exodus 30:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A cubit ſhall bee the length] That in Ezekiel, Chap. 41.22. is much larger, as ſetting forth the ſervice of God under the Goſpel.

entries.title: Exodus 30:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Overlaie it with pure gold] Shadowing Chriſt's Deïtie, yielding glorie to his humanitie. [A crown of gold round about] To ſhew, that Devotion is a rich roial virtue, beſt beſeeming the beſt Princes.

entries.title: Exodus 30:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Where I will meet with thee] To give oracles and anſwers of Mercie. God ſtill meeteth him that rejoiceth and worketh righteouſneſs. Iſa. 64.5.

entries.title: Exodus 30:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Shall burn thereon ſweet incenſ] Facium & veſpae favos. The Heathens had the like cuſtom; Verbenáſque adole pingues, (Virgil.) & maſcula thura.

entries.title: Exodus 30:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And when Aaron lighteth the lamps] To ſhew, that our praiers muſt bee made according to the light and direction of God's Word, leſt wee ask wee know not what, and worſhip wee know not how.

entries.title: Exodus 30:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: An attonement upon the horns of it] Pardon muſt bee ſought for the defects found in praiers; as Nehemiah craved mercie for his Reformations.

entries.title: Exodus 30:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That there bee no plague] David in numbering the people, neglected this dutie: thence the plague.

entries.title: Exodus 30:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: half a ſhekel] Towards the making of the Tabernacle; and as an amercing himſelf for his ſin, that ſubjected him to utter deſtruction. Verſ 15.

entries.title: Exodus 30:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The rich ſhall not give more] They are both of a price, becauſ in ſpirituals they are equal. 2 Pet. 1.1.

entries.title: Exodus 30:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That it may bee a memorial] A perpetual poll-monie, in token of homage and ſubjection to the Almightie.

entries.title: Exodus 30:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Between the Tabernacle and the Altar] The laver and Altar ſituated in the ſame court, ſignified the ſame; as the water and blood iſſuing out of Chriſt's ſide; viz. the neceſſarie concurrence of Juſtification and Sanctification in all that ſhall bee ſaved.

entries.title: Exodus 30:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For Aaron and his ſons] Here they were to waſh, before they praied for the people. (Heb. 10.22.) Wee muſt firſt make our own peace with God before wee take upon us to intercede for others. So did David. Pſalm 25.22. and Pſalm 51.18, 19. So wee are adviſed to do. Lam. 3.39, 40.

entries.title: Exodus 30:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That they die not] Com not to an untimelie end, as they did. Lev. 10.1, 2.

entries.title: Exodus 30:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And thou ſhalt annoïnt the Tabernacle] So to conſecrate the ſame to God's ſervice, and to ſet forth how joifully and gladly men ſhould ſerv the Lord.

entries.title: Exodus 30:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Whatſoever toucheth them] So are all thoſe annointed holie, that by a lively faith touch the Lord Chriſt.

entries.title: Exodus 30:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Aaron and his ſons] Thoſe onely that ſucceeded him in the office of High-prieſt. Lev. 4.3, 5, 16. and 16.32.

entries.title: Exodus 30:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ʋpon man's fleſh] A Latine Poſtiller hence infer's, in an hyperbolical ſenſ, that Prieſts are Angels, not having humane fleſh.

entries.title: Exodus 30:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Whoſoever compoundeth anie thing like it] Holie things muſt not bee profaned on pain of death. No people ſo abuſe Scripture to common and ordinarie uſe as the Jews do.

entries.title: Exodus 31:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: GOd gift's whomſoever hee call's to anie emploiment.

entries.title: Exodus 31:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To deviſe cunning works] All skill in lawful callings, whether manual or mental, is of God. Iſa. 28.26.

entries.title: Exodus 31:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And in cutting of ſtones] Moſes might well doubt where hee ſhould finde fit work-men among thoſe brick-makers for Egypt.

entries.title: Exodus 31:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I have given with him] Two is better then one; four eies ſee more then two: God uſually therefore coupleth his agents. See the Note on Mat. 10.2, 3. Luke 10.1.

entries.title: Exodus 31:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Verily my ſabbaths yee ſhall keep] q. d. Though this Sanctuarie-work is to bee don, yet it ſhall bee no Sabbath's-daies work. The good women in the Goſpel forbare on the Sabbath to annoint the dead bodie of our Saviour, reſting according to the Commandement. [For it is a ſign] And withal an effectual means to conveigh holineſs into the heart.

entries.title: Exodus 31:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For it is holie unto you] Hence the Hebrews gather (but falſly) that onely Iſraël was charged with the Sabbath-daie, and not the nations of the world. But the Sabbath was kept before Iſraël was born.

entries.title: Exodus 31:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Whoſoever doth anie work] A certain Indian that had been taught by the Engliſh, coming by, and ſeeing one of the Engliſh profaning the Lord's daie, by felling of a tree, ſaid to him, (New-England's firſt-fruits.) Do ye not know that this is the Lord's daie in Maſſaquſets (one of the Engliſh Plantations) much machet man, that is, verie wicked man, why break you God's daie?

entries.title: Exodus 31:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Written with the finger of God] Of the Decalogue, above all other holie Writ, God ſeem's to ſaie as Paul, Philem. 19. Behold, I have written it with mine own hand: i. e. by mine own power and operation.

entries.title: Exodus 32:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Aron might make a Calf, but the people made it a God, by adoring it. Qui fingit ſacros auro vel marmore vultus (Martial.) Non facit ille Deos; qui rogat, iste facit.

entries.title: Exodus 32:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Break off your golden ear-rings] Hereby hee hoped to break their deſign: but all in vain: for they were mad upon their Idols. Jer. 59.38.

entries.title: Exodus 32:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Brake off the golden ear-rings] which they had got of the Egyptians. Exod. 12.35. To make uſe of Heathen Autors for oſtentation, is to make a Calf of the treaſure gotten out of Egypt.

entries.title: Exodus 32:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A molten Calf] In imitation of the Egyptian Idol Apis, a Pied-bullock. A man may paſs through Ethiopia unchanged; but hee cannot dwel there, and not bee diſcolored.

entries.title: Exodus 32:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A feaſt to Jehovah] Whom theſe Idolaters pretended to worſhip in the golden Calf, as did alſo Jehu. 2 King. 10.16, 29. 2 Chron. 11.15. and as the Papiſts at this daie: but with what face can ſom of their Rabbins excuſe this people from Idolatrie?

entries.title: Exodus 32:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Roſe up to plaie] To dance about the Calf. Now, if they were ſo cheared and ſtrengthned by thoſe baneful bits, thoſe murthering morſels; ſhould not wee much more by God's ſpiritual proviſions, to dance as David did, to do his work with all our might?

entries.title: Exodus 32:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For thy people which thou broughteſt] God will own them no longer; they are now diſ-covenanted. The Saints by groſs ſins may loſe their jus aptitudinale, non jus haereditarium, their fitneſs for God's Kingdom; they may ſin away all their comfortables.

entries.title: Exodus 32:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They have turned aſide quickly] Moſes's back was but newly turned, as it were. I marvel that you are ſo ſoon removed, &c. Gal. 1.6. See the Note there. When wee have ſpent all our winde on our people, their hearts will bee ſtill apt to bee carried away with every winde of doctrine.

entries.title: Exodus 32:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A ſtiff-necked people] And ſo they are ſtill to this verie daie. Hierom complain's that in his time they thrice a daie curſed Chriſt in their Synagogue, (Hieron. in Iſa. lib. 12. cap 49. tom. 5. & lib. 14 cap. 42.) and cloſed up their praiers with Maledic Domine Nazaraeis. They are thought to adviſe moſt of that miſchief, which the Turk put's in execution againſt Chriſtians. They counterfeit Chriſtianitie in Portugal even to the degree of Prieſthood, and think they may do it, either for the avoiding of danger, or increaſing their ſubſtance. There are verie few of them that turn Chriſtians in good earneſt: Adeò in cordibus eorum radices fixit pertinacitas, (River. Jeſuita Vapul. 322.) So ſtubborn they are to this daie, and ſtiff-necked, their necks are wholly poſſeſt with an iron ſinew.

entries.title: Exodus 32:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let mee alone] God is fain to beſpeak his own freedom: As if Moſes his devotion were ſtronger then God's indignation. Great is the power of Praier; able, after a ſort, to transfuſe a dead Palſie into the hand of Omnipotencie.

entries.title: Exodus 32:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Lord, why doth thy wrath] God offered Moſes a great fortune. Ver. 10. Hee tendering God's glorie refuſed, and make's requeſt for the people. It is the ingenuitie of Saints to ſtudie God's ends more then their own, and drown all ſelf-reſpects in his glorie.

entries.title: Exodus 32:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Repent of this evil] God's repenting is mutatio rei,non Dei; effect[ilegible]s, non affectùs; facti, non conſilii; not a charge of his will, but of his work.

entries.title: Exodus 32:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Remember Abraham] Here Moſes neither invocateth the Patriarchs, nor allegeth their merits, but mind's God of his promiſe to them, and preſſeth the performance. In the want of other Rhethorick, let Chriſtians in their praiers urge this with repetition, Lord thou hast promiſed, thou haſt promiſed. Put the promiſes into ſuit, and you may have any thing. God cannot denie himſelf.

entries.title: Exodus 32:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the Lord repented] See ver. 12. Moſes here had a hard pull, but hee carried it.

entries.title: Exodus 32:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Written on both their ſides] See the like in other myſtical books. Ezek. 2.10. Rev. 5.1.

entries.title: Exodus 32:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The work of God] The greater was the peoples loſs, brought upon them by their ſin.

entries.title: Exodus 32:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And when Ioſhua] who had waited in ſom part of the Mount, the return of his Maſter.

entries.title: Exodus 32:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And Moſes's anger waxed hot] Meekneſs in this caſe had been no better then mopiſhneſs. How bleſſedly blown up was Moſes here. [Hee ſaw the Calf, and the dancing] One Calf about another. It was a cuſtom among Papiſts, that men ſhould run to the Image of St Vitus, (Joh. Manli. loc. com. 187.) and there they ſhould dance all daie, uſque ad animae deliquium, till they fainted and fell into a ſwoun.

entries.title: Exodus 32:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And hee took the Calf] Wee may all wiſh ſtill as Ferus did, that wee had ſom Moſes to take away the evils of our times: Nam non unum tantùm vitulum, ſed multoshabemus, Wee have not one, but many ſuch Calvs.

entries.title: Exodus 32:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What did this people unto thee] The people ſinned by precipitancie; Aaron by popularitie.

entries.title: Exodus 32:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That they are ſet on miſchief] The whole world is ſo. 1 Ioh. 2.16. and 5.19. Quomodo Plautus, In fermento tota jacet uxor.

entries.title: Exodus 32:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Wee wot not what, &c.] See the danger of nonreſidencie.

entries.title: Exodus 32:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There came out this Calf] A verie poor excuſe. Somthing hee would have ſaid if hee had known what. Here hee hid his ſin as Adam. Iob 31.33. beeing too much his childe.

entries.title: Exodus 32:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Aaron bad made them naked] As Aaron's ingraving inſtrument write's down his ſin: ſo the Confeſſion of other more ingenious Jews proclaim's the Iſraëlites, ſaying that No puniſhment befalleth thee, O Iſraël, (Moſ. Gerund.) in which there is not an ounce of this Calf.

entries.title: Exodus 32:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let him com] This word through haſte and earneſtneſs Moſes omitteth. The Chaldee and Greek verſions ſupplie it.

entries.title: Exodus 32:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Slaie ever[ilegible]e man his brother] Not all that they met with, (for ſo they might have ſlain the innocent) but all that were chief in the tranſgreſſion. In the war againſt the Waldenſes in France, the Pope's great Armie took one populous Citie and put to the ſword ſixtie thouſand, among whom were manie of their own Catholicks. For Arnoldus the Ciſtercian Abbat (beeing the Pope's Legat in this great war) commanded the ſouldiers ſaying, Caedite eos: novit enim Dominus qui ſunt ejus: (Caeſar. Heiſterbuchenſis hiſt. lib. 5. cap. 2[ilegible].) Kill them one with another: for the Lord knoweth who are his. This was fine Popiſh Juſtice.

Ner. 28. About three thouſand] Chieftains and ring-leaders.

entries.title: Exodus 32:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Conſecrate your ſelvs] Regain that bleſſing which your father Levi loſt. Gen. 49.5, 7.

entries.title: Exodus 32:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And now I will go up unto the Lord] As angrie as hee was, hee could praie for them: As when our children, through their own fault have got ſom ſickneſs, for all our angrie ſpeeches wee go to the Phyſician for them.

entries.title: Exodus 32:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Made them gods of gold] Sin muſt not bee confeſſed in the lump onely, and by whole ſale, but wee muſt inſtance the particulars.

entries.title: Exodus 32:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Blot mee I praie thee] God never revealed his love to Moſes more, then when hee thus earneſtly praied for God's people. Joab never pleaſed David better, then when hee made interceſſion for Abſolom.

entries.title: Exodus 32:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Blot out] Cut him out of the roll of the living.

entries.title: Exodus 32:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I will viſit] I will paie them home for the new and the old.

entries.title: Exodus 32:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
